articles.title: Sea-Intelligence: Increased Service Instability
articles.summary: Since the pandemic, we have seen a severe escalation in liner service instability across major deep‑sea trades, caused by increases in blank sailings, services phasing in/out, vessels delayed into the following week, and ad‑hoc extra‑loaders. articles.body: Since the pandemic, we have seen a severe escalation in liner service instability across major deep‑sea trades, caused by increases in blank sailings, services phasing in/out, vessels delayed into the following week, and ad‑hoc extra‑loaders. We measure the instability as the standard deviation of the number of weekly offered services, but express it as the percentage of the average number of services, to account for the change in number of offered services. Figure 1 shows the relative standard deviation of the post‑pandemic period (2020‑2026) in excess of the pre‑pandemic (2013‑2019) baseline. Source: Sea-Intelligence.com, Sunday Spotlight, issue 789 The most profound operational disruptions are currently concentrated on the Asia‑Europe trade lane, with Asia‑North Europe seeing an massive 78% increase in weekly service instability, while Asia‑Mediterranean recorded a 71% increase. The Transpacific network has also reached higher baseline of service instability, although it has absorbed the turbulence slightly better than Asia‑Europe. Service instability on the Asia‑North America East Coast trade lane recorded the smallest comparative growth, increasing by 26%, while Asia‑North America West Coast saw a 48% increase. This increased destabilization of liner networks causes cascading negative consequences for both cargo owners and maritime infrastructure. For shippers, this constant weekly shifting in available capacity makes it incredibly hard to plan their supply chains. More importantly, these unexpected changes create major bottlenecks at the arrival ports. When the number of arriving vessels and containers constantly goes up and down, it greatly increases the risk of sudden port congestion. This congestion can then lead to longer waiting times for vessels, in turn worsening schedule reliability and lengthening transit times. Alan Murphy, CEO, Sea-Intelligence

articles.title: Ammonia-Powered Bulk Carrier Takes on Green Fuel in Australian First
articles.summary: Australia has completed its first green ammonia bunkering operation involving an ammonia-powered bulk carrier, marking another step toward bringing alternative fuels into commercial shipping. The operation took place earlier this...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network The ammonia-powered bulk carrier Mineral Europa receives green ammonia during a ship-to-ship bunkering operation at the Port of Port Hedland, Australia. Photo: Fortescue Australia has completed its first green ammonia bunkering operation involving an ammonia-powered bulk carrier, marking another step toward bringing alternative fuels into commercial shipping. The operation took place earlier this week at the Port of Port Hedland in Western Australia, where the 300-meter Mineral Europa received certified green ammonia from a bunker vessel before entering port to load iron ore bound for China. The vessel, described as the world’s first ammonia-powered dry bulk carrier, is operated by CMB.TECH and chartered to Australian mining giant Fortescue. According to a joint announcement from Fortescue, Pilbara Ports and CMB.TECH , the ship-to-ship transfer took approximately two hours and was completed successfully at 8:42 a.m. local time. The operation required extensive planning, including vessel compatibility assessments, ammonia dispersion modeling, emergency response procedures, and additional marine support. Port authorities said the trial proceeded only after all safety and operational requirements had been met. The successful bunkering is particularly significant for the iron ore trade, which relies heavily on large bulk carriers transporting Australian exports to Asian steelmakers. Fortescue is seeking to reduce emissions from those voyages by introducing ammonia-powered vessels and developing a reliable supply of green marine fuel. Unlike conventional marine fuels, ammonia contains no carbon and produces no carbon dioxide when used as fuel. Its overall emissions benefits, however, depend on how it is produced and on controlling other emissions, including nitrous oxide. Ammonia’s toxicity also presents additional challenges for ship operators, ports and bunker suppliers. Fortescue Metals CEO Dino Otranto said the operation demonstrated that ammonia bunkering is moving beyond small-scale testing toward practical use in major commercial ports. “Industry has moved ahead of regulation to prove the technology,” Otranto said. He added that policy certainty and long-term fuel purchasing commitments would be needed to support further investment in green ammonia production and bunkering infrastructure. Fortescue has been an early supporter of ammonia as a marine fuel. In 2024, its Fortescue Green Pioneer completed ammonia-fueled propulsion trials in Singapore , demonstrating the technology aboard a converted offshore support vessel. The company has since expanded its commercial shipping ambitions through a partnership with CMB.TECH. In addition to Mineral Europa , Fortescue charters nine other vessels from the shipping group that can be converted to operate on ammonia in the future. The companies also announced an agreement earlier this year covering up to 12 ammonia-capable bulk carriers. The Port Hedland operation builds on an earlier ship-to-ship ammonia transfer trial at nearby Dampier in September 2024 , which helped establish procedures for handling ammonia between vessels. Pilbara Ports is now studying the development of a clean fuel bunkering hub in the region, with the latest trial expected to inform future operations. While ammonia-powered shipping still faces substantial hurdles involving fuel cost, availability, safety and regulatory standards, the Port Hedland operation demonstrates how the fuel could be supplied to large commercial vessels at one of the world’s busiest bulk export ports. The companies did not disclose the quantity of green ammonia transferred during the operation. articles.title: Finnish Court Jails Cargo Ship Captain, Crew Member for Baltic Sea Cable Sabotage
articles.summary: A Finnish court on Thursday jailed the Russian captain and an Azerbaijani crew member of the cargo ship Fitburg for aggravated sabotage over damage to two subsea telecommunications cables in the Gulf of Finland last year.

Finnish Police/Handout via REUTERS HELSINKI, Nov 5 (Reuters) – A Finnish court on Thursday jailed the Russian captain and an Azerbaijani crew member of the cargo ship Fitburg for aggravated sabotage over damage to two subsea telecommunications cables in the Gulf of Finland last year. Finland on December 31 seized the vessel in the Gulf of Finland while it was en route from Russia to Israel, on suspicion that it had damaged cables running from Helsinki to Estonia. The Helsinki District Court sentenced the captain to 3 years and 6 months in prison and the crew member to 2 years and 10 months. It said in a statement the two acted intentionally when the ship dragged an anchor chain and anchor shank along the seabed for around 130 km (81 miles). Finland has intensified efforts to protect its undersea infrastructure following a string of incidents affecting cables and pipelines in the Baltic Sea since 2022, including a vessel-boarding drill it conducted in September. The captain will appeal the verdict, while the crew member has not yet decided whether to do so, their respective lawyers said. The court also ordered the two defendants to jointly pay around €1.9 million ($2.1 million) in damages, and ordered the captain to pay about €85,000 more, the verdict showed. The seized vessel, sailing under Saint Vincent and the Grenadines’ flag, was en route from the Russian port of St Petersburg to Israel at the time of the incident. The ship has since been released. The defendants, who have remained in Finland subject to travel bans, have denied any wrongdoing and have challenged Finland’s jurisdiction in the case. The 14 crew members of the vessel were nationals of Russia, Georgia, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan, investigators have said. articles.title: Seven Shadow Fleet Tankers Spoof AIS to Hide Novorossiysk Voyages
articles.summary: Sanctioned Tankers Fake Their Positions Near the Bosphorus A cluster of seven sanctioned Russian tankers were found to have routinely and deliberately manipulated AIS over the past 90 days to falsely claim they were drifting off the Black Sea close to the Bosphorus entrance. articles.body: Seven Shadow Fleet Tankers Spoof AIS to Hide Novorossiysk Voyages in International Shipping News 06/11/2026 Sanctioned Tankers Fake Their Positions Near the Bosphorus A cluster of seven sanctioned Russian tankers were found to have routinely and deliberately manipulated AIS over the past 90 days to falsely claim they were drifting off the Black Sea close to the Bosphorus entrance. The tankers were instead identified by Windward clandestinely sailing for the Russian oil terminal of Novorossiysk to load oil, hugging the Black Sea coastline to try and avoid Ukrainian drone attacks. Satellite Imagery Exposes the Tankers Sailing to Novorossiysk Windward used satellite imagery to locate the tankers. At the same time, the tankers manipulated their AIS, a process known as spoofing. They began the practice shortly after transiting the Bosporus to enter the Black Sea just outside Turkey’s territorial waters but within the country’s exclusive economic zone. The spoofing left tell-tale uneven tracks. Windward Identifies Seven Sanctioned Shadow Fleet Tankers The vessels identified were a Sierra Leone-flagged Suezmax tanker, a Russia-flagged Aframax, a Russia-flagged Aframax tanker, an Equatorial Guinea-flagged Suezmax, an Equatorial Guinea-flagged Aframax, a Comoros-flagged Suezmax, and a Russia-flagged Aframax tanker. All are sanctioned, shadow fleet vessels. Periods of GNSS manipulation lasted around 2-3 weeks, the duration for tankers to sail to Novorossiysk, load, and return. While many vessels are switching off their AIS for legitimate safety and security reasons in the Black Sea, Russian shadow fleet tankers are using deceptive shipping practices, including GNSS manipulation, to avoid targeting by Ukrainian drones. Russian Attacks Imperil Freedom of Navigation Across the Black Sea Maritime safety and security remain perilous amid escalating Russian attacks on cargo vessels using a special maritime corridor to load grain from Ukrainian ports, including at Odesa and the Danube River. The hostility and aggression have imperiled freedom of navigation for commercial shipping across the Azov and the Black Sea. Ukraine told the International Maritime Organization on October 2 that Russia carried out 25 serious attacks between June 6 and September 23, involving 22 commercial ships and three search and rescue tugs and causing 26 seafarer deaths. A further seven cargo ships were damaged in attacks attributed to Russia off Bulgaria and Romania just outside their territorial waters over October. Ukraine appears to have paused drone strikes on tankers since July, mainly focusing on land targets including refineries. Unconfirmed reports of Ukraine’s last attack on a ship were in early October, at Sochi. Source: Windward 2026-11-06 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Newbuilding Orders Piling Up in Hellenic Shipping News 06/11/2026 T he newbuilding market has remained very elevated over the past week, as owners have kept securing more orders. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Banchero Costa said that “newbuilding activity remained exceptionally strong this week, with a total of 51 vessels ordered across a broad spectrum of sectors including bulk carriers, containers, tankers and car carriers. Container and tanker contracting accounted for the majority of activity, while Chinese shipbuilders continued to dominate order intake, reflecting their leading position in the global newbuilding market. In the bulk carrier sector, Greek owner Lavinia Ship Management reportedly contracted 4x 212,000 dwt Newcastlemax bulk carriers at Zhoushan Changhong, with deliveries scheduled between March 2030 and September 2031. Fellow Greek owner Meadway Bulkers reportedly contracted 6x 64,500 dwt Ultramax bulk carriers at Nantong Xiangyu, with deliveries scheduled for 2029-2030 In the container sector, MSC reportedly returned to Shanghai Waigaoqiao for a further 3x 22,000 teu LNG dual-fuel containerships priced, with deliveries scheduled between March and December 2029. Additional feeder activity was reported at Chengxi Shipyard with an unidentified German owner ordering 4x 3,700 teu vessels, while Harbour Link Group contracted 2 coastal container vessels at Malaysia’s Sapor Shipyard”, the shipbroker said. articles.title: Inmarsat Maritime Safety Data Hub to help shipping weather the storm
articles.summary: Deep-sea shipping is an inherently hazardous enterprise and the many operational risks faced by vessels, cargo, and crew will likely never be eliminated entirely. Nevertheless, data can play a significant role in minimising the frequency and severity of incidents at sea. As the maritime threat landscape continues to...
articles.body: Inmarsat Maritime Safety Data Hub to help shipping weather the storm in International Shipping News 06/11/2026 D eep-sea shipping is an inherently hazardous enterprise and the many operational risks faced by vessels, cargo, and crew will likely never be eliminated entirely. Nevertheless, data can play a significant role in minimising the frequency and severity of incidents at sea. As the maritime threat landscape continues to evolve, so too must the quality of information available to the industry. Inmarsat Maritime recently launched the Maritime Safety Data Hub, which combines Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS) call data with an industry-first analysis of maritime safety broadcasts. Complementing this unique dataset is a series of interviews with maritime safety experts conducted by Inmarsat’s research partner, SeaFocus International, as part of the Safety Hub’s development. The resultant platform provides unprecedented insight into global shipping risk, moving beyond reporting individual incidents to identify patterns, trends, and the evolving impact of environmental hazards, operational pressures, and geopolitical instability on safety at sea. John Dodd, Head of Maritime Safety at Inmarsat Maritime Managing weather hazards Among the 106,975 maritime safety broadcasts made in 2025, 2.6% were marked ‘urgent’. Of these, Inmarsat analysis identified 84.6% as related to weather, with storms and gales representing 75% and 20% of meteorological hazards, respectively. Despite accounting for just 4% of these hazards, cyclones were responsible for over 99% of urgent weather messages, reflecting their disproportionate impact on safety. Inmarsat’s findings also revealed that, on average, around 10 weather warnings were broadcast in the 12 hours preceding each distress event – offering a clear correlation between hazardous meteorological conditions and increased operational risk. However, as Olli Soininen, Head of Programmes at Fintraffic VTS, pointed out in his contribution to Inmarsat’s research, a storm does not create exactly the same risk for every vessel, with a ship’s size, type, capabilities, route, and operating conditions all influencing potential outcomes. Information that takes more of this context into account could help the master decide whether to continue, alter course, delay a voyage, or take another action, he added. Having access to more granular data on a vessel’s vulnerability to extreme weather can therefore help crew avoid distress situations. Targeted training is also vital. According to Professor Momoko Kitada, Academic Dean and Head of Maritime Education and Training at the World Maritime University, simulators can recreate diverse scenarios, vessel sizes, vessel types, geographic regions, and passages. Doing so enables crew to practise responding to challenging situations without having to wait for such circumstances to occur at sea, where an inexperienced seafarer may be more inclined to send a distress alert, she said. Persistent challenges, evolving risks While Inmarsat received fewer GMDSS calls in 2025 (741) than in 2023 (788) and 2024 (801), the three-year trend remains broadly consistent with historical averages, reflecting how established safety challenges persist even as new risks emerge. In 2025, distress activity remained concentrated among large commercial vessels operating along major global trade and energy corridors. Responsible for the most GMDSS calls by vessel type were tankers (203), bulk carriers (105), dry cargo vessels (83), offshore vessels (75), and container ships (54), with these results largely consistent with those of the preceding two years. Laurent Parenté, Director General of the International Mobile Satellite Organization (IMSO), said that the consistency in Inmarsat’s GMDSS data does not necessarily imply a lack of improvement. Instead, he explained, “it just means that the risk is evolving”. For example, as geopolitical tensions flare, sanctions, tariffs, and route disruptions are reshaping trade patterns and extending voyages for tankers, dry cargo vessels, and container ships. This in turn increases fuel consumption, crew workloads, and vessel exposure. Shipping has also been caught in the crosshairs of digital warfare. Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) spoofing and signal jamming are undermining operators’ situational awareness in strategic waterways, particularly for tankers and container ships. Alongside traditional concerns such as weather, machinery failure, and navigational incidents, these emerging threats add new layers of complexity to commercial shipping operations. Contributing to Inmarsat’s research, Simon Osborne, Co-Founder of MarinAI, described GNSS jamming and spoofing as “very significant” issues that are “rapidly becoming more widespread in the maritime domain”. He explained that the phenomena cause “electronic fog”, which can reduce a navigator’s confidence in the information presented by onboard systems. One solution, he suggested, may involve seafarers relearning and honing the “old navigational techniques” that technological progress has made less prominent. In this way, mariners would be better equipped to navigate safely in the increasingly common event of GNSS interference. A powerful new layer of maritime intelligence The Inmarsat Maritime Safety Data Hub will enable the industry to better understand the factors affecting maritime safety and adopt a more proactive approach to risk management, commented John Dodd, Head of Maritime Safety at Inmarsat Maritime. “The value of maritime safety information lies in giving ships and shipping operators the time to make informed decisions,” he said. “Whether the threat is extreme weather or geopolitical instability, early awareness enables crews to take action that protects lives, vessels, and cargo.” Ultimately, by combining weather information with distress call data, Inmarsat’s “powerful new layer of maritime intelligence” can help shipping address its persistent and evolving safety challenges, Dodd concluded. Source: Inmarsat Maritime Tops 2026-11-06 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

Average crude oil prices continued to climb, while further attacks, including along the west coast of Saudi Arabia, impacted exports from the LPG terminal at Yanbu. Longer voyage times and increased reliance on U.S. supply to Asia kept freight rates elevated. Panama Canal delays and high transit fees were also observed during Q3 2026, particularly for northbound transits, amid congestion, low water levels and reductions in daily transit capacity. As a result, supply chain economics remained challenging. Despite higher crude prices, propane and butane prices declined in Q3 2026 on both an absolute and crude-relative basis. In the U.S., strong export demand was offset by robust NGL production and elevated inventories, keeping propane below 40% of WTI. Butane showed greater strength as buyers increased demand for split cargoes to meet retail requirements in South and Southeast Asia. Panama Canal inefficiencies and longer trade routes due to ballasting around the Cape of Good Hope contributed to slightly lower quarter-over-quarter volumes, but U.S. export facilities still did not operate at full capacity, highlighting the relative shortage of shipping supply. Overall, Chinese LPG imports in Q3 2026 are estimated to have been approximately one MMT higher than in the previous quarter, while positive variable margins for PDH operations continued to support LPG demand. At the same time, robust U.S.–Asia export flows increased ton-mile demand as U.S. cargoes replaced lost Middle East volumes. Freight markets were further supported by elevated war-risk insurance premiums, higher bunker prices, Panama Canal congestion, increased canal costs, and continued reluctance among shipowners to re-enter the Persian Gulf, resulting in significant operational inefficiencies and sustained upward pressure on freight rates despite gradual improvements in regional export flows. During Q3 2026, the global VLGC fleet expanded moderately with the delivery of eight new vessels. Looking ahead, a further 160 VLGCs/VLACs—equivalent to approximately 14.4 million cbm of carrying capacity—are scheduled for delivery through calendar year 2030, including 19 new orders placed during the third quarter. The average age of the global fleet now stands at approximately 11.7 years, while the combined VLGC/VLAC orderbook has increased to around 36.4% of the existing fleet. articles.summary: Global ocean container shipping spot rates are forecast to fall 30% in 2027, according to the Xeneta Ocean Outlook Report unveiled today by Chief Analyst Peter Sand to more than 800 industry leaders from the world’s largest shippers and logistics service providers gathered at the annual Xeneta Summit in Munich....
articles.body: Xeneta Summit: Analysts forecast ocean freight spot rates to fall 30% in 2027 as Red Sea return sees capacity flooding back in International Shipping News 06/11/2026 G lobal ocean container shipping spot rates are forecast to fall 30% in 2027, according to the Xeneta Ocean Outlook Report unveiled today by Chief Analyst Peter Sand to more than 800 industry leaders from the world’s largest shippers and logistics service providers gathered at the annual Xeneta Summit in Munich. Xeneta – the leading neutral ocean and air freight rate intelligence solution – includes the following market fundamentals and forecasts in the Ocean Outlook 2027: • Global demand growth slowing to between 2.5% and 4% • Global fleet growth of 6.8% within a range of 5.4% to 8.3% • Global average spot rate to fall 30% • Global average long term rate to fall 5% Both rate forecasts are full-year 2027 averages against a Q3 2026 baseline. While Sand, pictured, told the Xeneta Summit the fundamentals point to softening rates in 2027, he warned it is not guaranteed. Peter Summit He said: “Rates were expected to soften in each of the past three years before seismic shocks sent them spiralling in the opposite direction – the Red Sea Crisis in 2024, the US tariffs in 2025 and the Hormuz Crisis in 2026. Supply growth will outrun demand in 2027, but market fundamentals are easily overpowered by major supply chain shocks and it would be foolish to rule that out in 2027. “The Transpacific trade to US West Coast spiked 343% between 28 February and 31 October this year, with triple-digit percentage increases seen across all Far East fronthauls. These are massive freight cost increases, but this is made even more extraordinary given the market fundamentals suggested an easier year for shippers heading into 2026.” Red Sea return is pivotal to falling rates The return of container shipping to the Red Sea and Suez Canal is central to the Xeneta forecast for 2027 following a significant ramping up of services transiting the region in recent months. In October 2026, carriers committed 467,297 TEU of weekly capacity to the Red Sea. While this is 50% of the pre-crisis level in August 2023, it is roughly double the offered capacity compared to the end of August 2026. The return of networks to the Suez Canal releases capacity absorbed by longer diversions around the Cape of Good Hope, with 599k TEU already released. This is in addition to forecasted global fleet growth of 6.8% in 2027. Carriers are due to take delivery of 2.9m TEU of new capacity next year and demolish 0.5m TEU. This follows 4.9% fleet growth in 2026. Sand said: “The Red Sea is pivotal to ocean container shipping in 2027 because it offers both sides of the coin. If there is a full return, freight rates could plummet. We could also be faced with the opposite extreme if a deterioration in the security situation in the Red Sea forces carriers to revert to Cape of Good Hope diversions. This would bring chaos to ocean networks and upward pressure on rates. “The significant ramping up of Red Sea services in recent months should not distract from the fragility of the geo-political situation in the wider Middle East. It will not take much to ignite the situation again and then the house of cards comes falling down. “This forecast should also be seen against the backdrop of appalling schedule reliability in 2026. Global on time arrivals were 27% in Q3 with Far East to Europe collapsing to just 4% in September. We may see a rebound in early 2027, but it is coming from a very low bar.” Demand growth to slow in 2027 with weaker peak season Global container shipping demand will grow between 2.5% and 4% in 2027, down from 4.7% in the first eight months of 2026. The demand growth in 2026 was built on frontloading as shippers looked to protect supply chains from the ripple effects of disruption in the Strait of Hormuz and rising fuel costs. Xeneta expects a slower start to 2027 followed by a weaker peak season. Sand said: “Supply chain shocks have distorted the rhythm of container shipping. Demand has been strong in 2026, but this growth will be difficult to sustain in 2027 as shippers draw down the inventories built up in 2026 against headwinds of more modest consumer appetite for containerized goods.” Be prepared for the unknown Sand reiterated the requirement for shippers to be ready for the unexpected in 2027, both in terms of supply chain resilience and freight budgets, with some threats already on the horizon. He said: “Low water levels in the Panama Canal could see restrictions enforced and shippers forced to pay a premium to secure timely transits. With the Suez Canal – the world’s other critical artery for maritime trade – already compromised, there isn’t too much slack in the system to manage further supply chain shocks.” Source: Xeneta Tops 2026-11-06 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Iran says five tankers and tugboat caught fire in Hormuz in International Shipping News 06/11/2026 Five oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards and army said in separate statements, according to local media on Thursday. Since the outbreak of the Iran war in late February, Tehran has severely restricted traffic through the strategic waterway, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil consumption. It regularly attacks ships it accuses of transiting without its authorization. The United States military has in response imposed a blockade on Iranian ports and helped tankers travel the strait. “Last night… a large oil tanker attempting to pass through the illegal passageway south of the Strait of Hormuz suffered a fire after striking a mine and was brought to a halt,” the Guards told Fars news agency. “Another supertanker was halted by a massive fire while exiting the eastern Strait of Hormuz. A tugboat that had approached the supertanker to extinguish the fire also caught fire,” the Guards said. The Iranian army later said three more tankers were hit by naval mines. “Early this morning, a violating oil tanker — navigating through an unsafe area east of the Strait of Hormuz — caught fire and came to a halt after striking a naval mine,” the army said, according to the official IRNA news agency. “Today at around noon, two more oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire in the unsafe waters east of the Strait of Hormuz,” said another army statement carried by IRNA. There has been no confirmation of the incidents from maritime officials. British monitor UKMTO reported a tanker being struck by “two unidentified projectiles” around 50 nautical miles (90 kilometers) off the north coast of Qatar, without providing details on any damage or casualties. That area is around 500 kilometers west of Hormuz, in the center of the Gulf. Fars also reported that the IRGC navy’s electronic warfare unit had taken control of two LUCAS drones, a US-developed model whose name is short for Low-cost Uncrewed Combat Attack System. Last month, the US military said it had helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil via Hormuz since the summer. Source: AFP 2026-11-06 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Fujairah’s LSMGO premium over Singapore widens by around $180/mt since September in International Shipping News 06/11/2026 Fujairah’s LSMGO price stood around $430/mt above Singapore’s this week, up from around $250/mt at the start of September. Fujairah’s LSMGO monthly average reached around $1,720/mt in October, the highest since November 2021. The port’s premium over Singapore was around $460/mt on 19 October. Supplies of LSMGO and HSFO at the UAE port remain limited, and vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted amid US-Iran tensions, a regional source said. Fujairah’s fuel oil stocks averaged 9% lower in October so far than across September, Fujairah Oil Industry Zone (FOIZ) and S&P Global data showed. Middle distillate stocks fell 27,000 bbls, to 2.40 million bbls. A market source said Fujairah is vulnerable to sudden shifts in availability due to reduced barge capacity, despite muted demand amidst reginal escalations and vessel attacks. The source said MGO is particularly exposed to a global diesel shortage, with Asian imports of light and middle distillates still below pre-war levels in October, in addition to constrained Middle Eastern refined-product supplies. Fujairah’s VLSFO price traded at a discount to Singapore’s of up to around $20/mt on each weekday from 27 October to 2 November. Singapore’s price reached around $1,000/mt on 30 October, as fuel oil inventories tightened and supply flows fell. Last week, VLSFO lead times at the port started at around 13 days, with some suppliers recommending more than three weeks. Singapore’s residual fuel oil inventories averaged 6% lower in October than in September. The gap reversed on 3 November, when Fujairah’s VLSFO price rose around $20/mt and Singapore’s fell around $20/mt. Fujairah’s VLSFO now trades at a premium of around $20/mt over Singapore, against around $50/mt on 1 September. VLSFO availability at Fujairah has improved, a regional source said. Source: By Tuhin Roy, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news/ 2026-11-06 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Global trade is growing. The capacity it needs doesn’t stop at the quay in Port News 06/11/2026 A container terminal can handle more cargo than ever before and still leave its customers waiting. Larger vessels and more efficient shipping networks have transformed how goods move across oceans. But the roads, railways and inland connections behind many ports have not kept pace. For much of the past 15 years, investment in landside infrastructure has lagged behind the changing demands of trade. That gap was easier to manage when there was room in the system. This year, geopolitical disruption, shifting trade routes and resilient cargo demand have exposed it. A port’s capacity and the capacity of the supply chain it serves are two different numbers.’’ The challenge looks different depending on where you stand. Europe’s Northern Range ports handled around 46 million TEU last year at almost 100% utilisation, and will need room for at least 53 million TEU by 2030 and 62 million by 2035. Across Africa, some gateways need entirely new capacity to support growing economies, while others need to make better use of what they already have. Igor van den Essen Chief Executive, Africa & Europe, APM TERMINALS The obvious response is to build. In many places we must, and we are. But I’m convinced that building alone won’t close the gap. A port’s capacity and the capacity of the supply chain it serves are two different numbers. Too often, we plan for the first and assume the second will follow. The pressure is only going to increase By 2030, around 900 container vessels above 15,000 TEU are expected to be in service, twice as many as today. Each call brings thousands of containers into a port within a short window, and every one of them has to move on through the same gates, rail terminals and roads. Trade routes are also becoming less predictable. Ports are built over decades on assumptions about where cargo comes from and where it goes. When those flows shift, as they have repeatedly in recent years, the infrastructure can’t move with them. Much of the world’s older port infrastructure, particularly in Europe, was designed for a different generation of ships. Modernising it while keeping cargo moving can be harder than building from scratch. And the pressure doesn’t end at the quay. In many ports, the tightest constraint is now the channel that limits vessel access, the rail connection that can’t take more cargo, or the road network already at its limit. Capacity inside and outside the fence Speed up the quay and, if nothing beyond it changes, you have simply moved the queue to the gate. Terminal operators can do a great deal within their own operations. Our hub terminals supporting the Gemini network, including Rotterdam, Bremerhaven, Algeciras and Tangier, now handle more than 70% more moves per hour than a decade ago. Equipment upgrades played a role, but vital parts of the improvement came from how we work: better planning, more consistent processes and removing bottlenecks one at a time. There is a limit, though. Speed up the quay and, if nothing beyond it changes, you have simply moved the queue to the gate. At Pier 400 in Los Angeles, the biggest terminal on the Western hemisphere with 6,000 daily truck arrivals, average truck turn times have fallen by 55% since 2023, to around 39 minutes, while rail moves have more than doubled. Every minute a truck isn’t waiting is time spent moving cargo inland to customers looking forward to its arrival. The minute-math and hours saved are tangible. Rijeka Gateway in Croatia shows what happens when terminal capacity and inland connections are developed together. A year after opening, trucks turn around in an average of 15 minutes, and new rail links connect the gateway to Serbia, Hungary and Austria. That is capacity created for businesses across Central Europe, not just for the terminal. And it can move cargo from over-utilised terminals in the North – to the south of the continent and closer to the customers. First vessel call at Rijeka Gateway Investment only works when the wider system works We are investing across our network because we believe in the long-term importance of the gateways we operate. Those investments deliver most when the infrastructure around them develops at the same pace. In Rotterdam, together with Hapag-Lloyd, we are adding 1,000 metres of deep-sea berth at Maasvlakte II, doubling its length. In Spain, we have extended our concession in Valencia and are investing in new capacity. Spanish ports can strengthen their position in global trade, but that depends on timely permitting and stronger rail connections inland. In Germany, we’re investing around €1 billion in Bremerhaven. What that delivers for German exporters depends just as much on improving access through the Weser, so larger vessels can call reliably. A terminal built for tomorrow’s vessels behind a channel built for yesterday’s is an opportunity half taken. None of this works if terminal operators, governments and infrastructure providers plan in isolation. There is little value in expanding a terminal years before the rail or road behind it is ready. Getting calls from bigger vessels to reduce the cost of doing trade is worth a little, if ships are waiting at the quay or capacity going inland is constrained. What we ask of our partners is straightforward. Plan the whole chain together, so that channels, rail and road are sequenced with terminal capacity rather than added years later. Make permitting predictable, particularly for modernisation projects at terminals that have to keep running while the work is done. And match long-term commitments with long-term certainty: concessions run for 30 to 50 years, and the frameworks around them need to support investment over that horizon. Building more capacity matters. Making sure it works together matters more. Building resilience before the next disruption None of us can predict the next disruption. But a supply chain already running at its limit turns small problems into big ones, while one that runs reliably has room to respond. This is crucial as a part of a nation’s critical infrastructure. So, I hope our industry spends less time asking how many new quays the world needs and more time asking where capacity is being lost today – and who needs to act to win it back. Building more capacity matters. Making sure it works together matters more. Source: APM Terminals 2026-11-06 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: The capacity it needs doesn’t stop at the quay in Port News 06/11/2026 A container terminal can handle more cargo than ever before and still leave its customers waiting.
Larger vessels and more efficient shipping networks have transformed how goods move across oceans.
But the roads, railways and inland connections behind many ports have not kept pace.

articles.title: ENGINE: Americas Bunker Fuel Availability Outlook
articles.summary: North America Bunker demand has been steady in Houston, a trader said. HSFO and LSMGO availability is normal, while a few suppliers have seen tight spots in VLSFO deliveries. articles.body: ENGINE: Americas Bunker Fuel Availability Outlook in International Shipping News 06/11/2026 North America Bunker demand has been steady in Houston, a trader said. HSFO and LSMGO availability is normal, while a few suppliers have seen tight spots in VLSFO deliveries. Recommended lead times for HSFO and LSMGO are 5-7 days, and VLSFO can be supplied with around seven days’ notice. The US Gulf Coast has entered its sea fog season, and dense fog could cause delays and disruptions at the port, the trader said. Earlier this week, the US Coast Guard warned that patchy fog could cut visibility on the lower Houston Ship Channel and Galveston Bay, mostly in the early mornings. Mobile Bay faces the highest sea fog risk in the region this week, with a high threat on Thursday and Friday that could cut visibility to 1 nautical mile or less. Brownsville and Corpus Christi are also expected to face a high threat on Sunday. Tampa, Pascagoula and Freeport, Texas, are expecting a moderate threat, mostly today and tomorrow. The risk is low at Galveston, Port Arthur, Lake Charles, Marsh Island, Port Fourchon, New Orleans and Venice. At the Galveston Offshore Lightering Area (GOLA) prompt availability is a bit tight, a source said. All three grades can be delivered with 5-7 days’ notice. Bunker deliveries at GOLA are made on a first-come, first-served basis and depend on the weather. High wind gusts of up to 23 knots and waves of up to 1.1 metres are forecast there on Saturday. Despite bunker demand remaining high in New York, availability of all three conventional fuel grades is good, with no severe tight spots reported. Recommended lead times for VLSFO and LSMGO are 2-4 days, and HSFO can be delivered with around five days’ notice. Distillate supply, which includes LSMGO, is expected to tighten at the port towards the end of the year and stay short until early next year, the source said. No weather disruption is expected in New York this week, with only light rain forecast on Thursday and Friday. Bunker demand has been strong at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, a trader said. Demand has held up even though HSFO, VLSFO and LSMGO are mostly priced at a premium to Houston and New York. Los Angeles has been the most expensive of the three ports for VLSFO and HSFO in every month this year, and the gap has widened. Its VLSFO averaged $294/mt more than Houston’s in October, up from $72/mt more in January. Its HSFO premium over Houston grew from $62/mt to $304/mt over the same period. VLSFO and HSFO availability is normal at Los Angeles, with recommended lead times of 5-8 days, the trader said. LSMGO can be delivered in less than five days. Last week, a feasibility study by the two ports found that annual methanol bunker demand at Los Angeles and Long Beach could reach 64,000-250,000 mt by 2030. The ports plan to invite proposals for alternative fuel bunker demonstrations by the end of this year. At Canada’s Vancouver, bunker demand is steady, a source said. All three grades are available with lead times of 4-8 days. Latin America and the Caribbean Availability of VLSFO and LSMGO is good in Panama’s Balboa and Cristobal, with recommended lead times of 3-5 days. However, HSFO is tight at the ports, and has typically needed lead times of over a week and up to 10 days, a source said. A few suppliers may be able to deliver sooner, depending on the enquiry. A new bunker supplier is expected to enter the Panama market next month, which should increase competition and give buyers more supply options at the ports, the source said. Thunderstorms could disrupt bunker deliveries at Balboa until Saturday. Deliveries there run on a first-come, first-served basis, and vessels with a confirmed transit schedule get priority. High wind gusts and thunderstorms could also disrupt deliveries at St. Eustatius on Friday and Saturday, with gusts of up to 22 knots forecast. Deliveries there are made at anchorage, where barges could face delays, and cruise ships get priority. Buyers looking for HSFO in the Colombian ports of Cartagena, Santa Marta and Barranquilla still need to consult suppliers first, as the grade is tight, a trader said. VLSFO and LSMGO have good availability, with the earliest delivery dates 3-4 days out. Singapore-based bunker supplier TFG Marine will offer bunker fuels at several Venezuelan ports, with local supplier Impordiesel handling physical deliveries. Only a handful of suppliers offer HSFO in Peru’s Callao, where the grade is tight and stems need prior consultation with suppliers, a trader said. VLSFO and LSMGO are in normal supply, with recommended lead times of 4-7 days depending on stem size. VLSFO and LSMGO availability is normal in Brazil’s Santos, where recommended lead times are 4-7 days, a trader tells ENGINE. Rio de Janeiro can supply all three grades, but HSFO is tight and buyers need to check with suppliers before ordering. VLSFO and LSMGO are in normal supply there, with lead times of 3-5 days. Paranagua, Belem and Vila do Conde have good VLSFO and LSMGO availability, with recommended lead times of under five days. Rio Grande has no LSMGO supply this week. VLSFO is available but tight for prompt delivery. Bunker availability remains tight at Argentina’s Zona Comun anchorage, where VLSFO and LSMGO both need lead times of over a week and up to 10 days, a source said. High wind gusts could disrupt bunker deliveries in Zona Comun on Saturday, with gusts of around 30 knots forecast. Deliveries are most likely to be suspended when winds exceed 20 knots near the anchorage location. articles.title: Arc Begins Battery-Electric Conversion of Long Beach Harbor Tug
articles.summary: Arc, a marine technology company, has begun engineering the battery-electric conversion of Harbor Sentinel, a 50-foot harbor tug owned and operated by Pacific Maritime Group (PMG). Supported by funding from the Port of Long Beach through its Technology Advancement Program (TAP) and SWIFT Program…
articles.body: Arc Begins Battery-Electric Conversion of Long Beach Harbor Tug Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 5, 2026 © PMG Arc, a marine technology company, has begun engineering the battery-electric conversion of Harbor Sentinel, a 50-foot harbor tug owned and operated by Pacific Maritime Group (PMG). Supported by funding from the Port of Long Beach through its Technology Advancement Program (TAP) and SWIFT Program, along with a Volkswagen Environmental Mitigation Trust grant administered by the Bay Area Air Quality Management District, the project will replace the tug’s twin diesel engines with an Arc electric powertrain. Naval architecture firm Glosten is leading vessel engineering. Following commissioning, Harbor Sentinel will return to work from PMG’s Long Beach terminal for a 12-month demonstration. The Harbor Sentinel joined PMG’s harbor fleet in 2023. The tug currently runs on two Cummins KT19 diesel engines producing 950 horsepower and carries 8,900 gallons of fuel. Its work includes moving barges and supporting construction and shipyard operations. In converting to electric power, the tug joins other efforts by the California Air Resources Board (CARB) to improve the air quality in California. Glosten completed a feasibility study and hull scan before engineering began. The firm is now adapting the vessel and designing onboard systems to meet applicable U.S. Coast Guard Subchapter M requirements. PMG will remove both diesel engines and install an integrated electric powertrain tailored to the existing vessel. The system includes a battery bank targeting 2 MWh of usable energy, electric motors and drivetrain, power electronics for the vessel’s existing AC equipment, updated helm controls and captain displays, and onboard charging with a DC fast-charge inlet. Telematics will support 24/7 remote monitoring. To accommodate the system, PMG in-house will widen the Sentinel 3.5’ and build a new deck, midbody, and pilothouse. Arc will integrate, commission and test the system, then support PMG’s crew on site and remotely after the tug returns to service. Arc will also prepare the technical documentation required for Coast Guard review of its systems and components. The Port of Long Beach’s Technology Advancement Program supports demonstrations of emerging technologies on working port equipment as part of the San Pedro Bay Ports Clean Air Action Plan. During the 12-month demonstration, Arc will collect data on performance, operations and charging, report results to the Port quarterly, and deliver a final report evaluating the technology and its potential for broader commercial adoption. This project compliments other conversion projects in the Port of Los Angeles. Through the Harbor Sentinel conversion, Arc and Pacific Maritime Group aim to demonstrate the technical and economic feasibility of repowering existing commercial vessels with electric propulsion systems.

articles.summary: The Trump administration has approved a $1 billion offshore crude oil export project off the coast of Louisiana, clearing a major regulatory hurdle for a facility designed to load some...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche The Trump administration has approved a $1 billion offshore crude oil export project off the coast of Louisiana, clearing a major regulatory hurdle for a facility designed to load some of the world’s largest oil tankers directly in the Gulf of Mexico. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced Thursday that the Maritime Administration (MARAD) has approved the deepwater port license application for Blue Marlin Offshore Port, a project capable of exporting up to 2 million barrels of crude oil per day. The facility will be located approximately 99 miles off Cameron Parish, Louisiana, in West Cameron Block 509. The project, developed by an affiliate of Energy Transfer, will use existing and converted offshore platform infrastructure connected to crude oil supply hubs in Texas and southwest Louisiana. Blue Marlin is designed to accommodate Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs), allowing the massive tankers to load crude directly in deep water rather than relying on more congested inland port facilities. The system will have a maximum loading rate of 80,000 barrels per hour. According to the Department of Transportation, the project is expected to support up to 1,052 construction jobs. “Building this port will unleash domestic production, create more than 1,000 good-paying construction jobs along the Gulf of America, and open vital supply lines to global markets,” Duffy said. The approval is the fourth deepwater port project cleared under the Trump administration, following the Texas GulfLink crude oil export project, Delfin LNG off Louisiana, and the $8.2 billion ST LNG project approved off Texas last week. Blue Marlin is also the second crude oil export project approved since President Trump issued his Unleashing American Energy executive order in January 2025. The decision comes as the administration moves to accelerate approvals for major offshore energy infrastructure projects. Just last week, MARAD announced approval of an $8.2 billion deepwater LNG export project off the Texas coast, saying changes to its licensing process had shortened the review timeline. Unlike that project, Blue Marlin has been working through the federal approval process for years. Its initial application was submitted in October 2020, and MARAD and the U.S. Coast Guard completed the project’s final environmental impact statement earlier this year. The offshore terminal will be supplied through a dedicated pipeline network connecting the Nederland Terminal area in Texas and other inland crude oil hubs to the offshore loading facility. The project is intended to expand U.S. crude export capacity while reducing the need for large tankers to navigate congested coastal waterways. By moving loading operations farther offshore, MARAD says the facility could also reduce vessel collision risks. MARAD Administrator Stephen Carmel said the approval demonstrated the agency’s ability to accelerate energy infrastructure development while maintaining safety standards. The decision follows a review involving the Coast Guard, other federal agencies, and the states of Texas and Louisiana. Separately, the Environmental Protection Agency proposed air permits for the facility in October. The administration did not announce a construction start date or expected completion timeline for Blue Marlin. Operating revenue remained broadly stable at US$201.6 million, compared with US$200.8 million in the second quarter. Net income increased from US$33.8 million,...
articles.body: SFL Corporation reported net income of US$37.4 million for the third quarter of 2026, while its fixed-rate charter backlog reached approximately US$5 billion. Operating revenue remained broadly stable at US$201.6 million, compared with US$200.8 million in the second quarter. Net income increased from US$33.8 million, while earnings per share rose from US$0.25 to US$0.26. The shipowner generated adjusted EBITDA of US$122 million during the quarter. Vessel charter hire contributed US$178 million, while its offshore drilling assets generated another US$23 million. SFL declared a quarterly dividend of US$0.22 per share, marking its 91st consecutive quarterly dividend. Containers generate US$85 million SFL’s containership portfolio generated US$85 million in revenue during the quarter. The segment operated for approximately 2,300 days and achieved 100% utilisation. Containerships account for 71% of SFL’s fixed-rate charter backlog. The company’s portfolio includes 32 container vessels, including ships that have been acquired but not yet delivered. The average remaining contract duration for the container fleet is 8.3 years, weighted by charter revenue and excluding extension options. SFL agreed seven-year charter extensions covering six 15,400 TEU containerships during the quarter. The extensions will begin when the vessels’ existing employment arrangements expire in 2028 and 2029. Newbuildings backed by long-term employment The company also confirmed the acquisition of two 8,800 TEU containership newbuildings. Both vessels are scheduled for delivery during the second half of 2027. The ships have secured minimum eight-year charters with a leading liner company. Their acquisition forms part of a wider investment package that also includes new Very Large Ammonia Carriers. SFL’s current portfolio comprises 66 maritime assets across the container, car carrier, tanker, gas carrier, dry bulk and offshore energy segments. The company said 58% of its fixed contracted revenue is linked to investment-grade counterparties. Its charter backlog excludes extension options, purchase or cancellation options and potential future profit-sharing income. Liquidity reaches US$272 million SFL ended the quarter with US$111.9 million in cash and cash equivalents. It also had US$160 million in undrawn credit facilities, taking total liquidity to approximately US$272 million. Remaining capital expenditure commitments stood at around US$1.7 billion. The company expects to fund these commitments through available cash and secured credit facilities. SFL also agreed to sell seven tanker vessels. The transactions are expected to generate aggregate net cash proceeds of approximately US$275 million, with deliveries to the new owners divided between the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027.

Photo: Kate Ciembronowicz/Orsted Danish offshore wind developer Ørsted has completed its 704-megawatt Revolution Wind project off the U.S. East Coast, marking a major milestone for a development that faced repeated shutdown orders from the Trump administration. The company announced Thursday that Revolution Wind reached commercial operations in October under its power purchase agreements with utilities in Rhode Island and Connecticut, following the installation of its final wind turbines in September. The project, a joint venture between Ørsted and Skyborn Renewables, consists of 65 offshore wind turbines capable of supplying enough electricity to power more than 350,000 homes in New England. Its completion represents a significant turnaround for a project that spent much of the past year fighting to stay under construction. The Trump administration first ordered work stopped in August 2025, citing national security concerns. A federal judge subsequently allowed construction to resume, but the administration issued another suspension order in December as part of a broader effort to halt five offshore wind projects under construction along the East Coast. As gCaptain reported in January , Ørsted challenged the second suspension in federal court, arguing that the project had already invested or committed billions of dollars after undergoing extensive federal permitting and review. At the time, Revolution Wind was approximately 87% complete. A federal judge later granted a preliminary injunction allowing work to proceed. The project began producing electricity earlier this year and installed its final turbine in September before reaching full commercial operations the following month. The milestone does not necessarily end the project’s regulatory challenges. The Interior Department sought court permission in October to reconsider its earlier approval of the wind farm’s construction and operations plan, raising further questions about the administration’s approach to already-operating offshore wind projects. For Ørsted, however, Revolution Wind’s completion comes as the company reports improving operating performance across its global portfolio. In its third-quarter earnings announcement , Ørsted said earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA), excluding new partnerships and cancellation fees, rose 19% to DKK 20.2 billion ($3.0 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, compared with DKK 17.0 billion a year earlier. Third-quarter EBITDA on the same basis climbed 72% to DKK 5.26 billion, helped by stronger wind conditions, higher electricity prices and increased generation from newly completed offshore wind farms. The company nevertheless recorded a third-quarter net loss of DKK 728 million, while profit for the first nine months fell to DKK 2.6 billion from DKK 6.5 billion. Ørsted attributed the decline largely to non-cash impairments associated with rising interest rates affecting its U.S. projects. “We continue to deliver on our strategic priorities, which is translating into consistent strong financial performance,” said CEO Rasmus Errboe. The company also reported progress at its other major U.S. offshore wind development, Sunrise Wind, where installation of all wind turbine foundations has been completed. The 924-megawatt project off New York remains under construction. Elsewhere, Ørsted said Germany’s Borkum Riffgrund 3 offshore wind farm had also reached commercial operations, while construction continued at projects in Taiwan, Poland and the United Kingdom. Ørsted maintained its full-year EBITDA guidance of more than DKK 28 billion, excluding new partnerships and cancellation fees, and lowered its expected gross investments for 2026 to DKK 45 billion to DKK 50 billion. The company said the reduction reflects changes in payment timing rather than lower overall project costs. The completion of Revolution Wind is particularly notable given the uncertainty surrounding the U.S. offshore wind industry. While the Trump administration has moved aggressively to restrict new development, projects already under construction have continued advancing through legal challenges and regulatory disputes. For Revolution Wind, those battles have now given way to commercial electricity production, even as questions remain about the future of offshore wind development in the United States. articles.title: General Dynamics Mission Systems Awarded $15m MEDUSA Contract Modification
articles.summary: General Dynamics Mission Systems announced it was awarded a $15 million contract modification to exercise options under a previously awarded contract for the Mining Expendable Delivery Unmanned Submarine Asset (MEDUSA).Building on the prototype…
articles.body: General Dynamics Mission Systems Awarded $15m MEDUSA Contract Modification Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 5, 2026 © General Dynamics Mission Systems General Dynamics Mission Systems announced it was awarded a $15 million contract modification to exercise options under a previously awarded contract for the Mining Expendable Delivery Unmanned Submarine Asset (MEDUSA). Building on the prototype, software and engineering work advanced under the July contract modification, this follow-on award continues MEDUSA's maturation and expands the program’s support infrastructure. MEDUSA is a submarine-launched delivery system that uses an expendable unmanned underwater vehicle (UUV) to deploy diverse payloads with precision. Purpose-built to meet the U.S. Navy's requirements for long-range offensive mining capability, the system offers flexibility to host additional payloads across a range of maritime missions. Work began in September 2026 and will continue through February 2028 at General Dynamics facilities in Quincy and Taunton, Massachusetts. The Naval Sea Systems Command, Washington Navy Yard, District of Columbia, is the contracting activity. General Dynamics has invested in its facilities and staff to support the growth of its UUV centers of excellence and advance undersea programs. These include the Center of Excellence for Research and Development, Prototyping, and Offshore Test in Quincy and the UUV Manufacturing and Assembly Center of Excellence in Taunton. Together, these sites provide an integrated path from concept through production. The Quincy facility supports rapid prototyping and in-water testing, while the Taunton facility provides the advanced manufacturing capacity to transition mature designs toward full-rate production. Alongside these investments, General Dynamics is working with suppliers to strengthen the industrial base and expand production capacity to meet the U.S. Navy’s future demands.

November 5, 2026 Overhead view of Katsa's new 54,000-square-foot gearbox assembly facility and warehouse that's currently under construction in Pirkkala, Finland. © Katsa Twin Disc, Inc. subsidiary Katsa announced that it is expanding its capacity with a 54,000-square-foot gearbox assembly facility and warehouse in Pirkkala, Finland, in response to a double-digit percentage year-over-year increase in demand. The new plant, expected to be fully operational by May 2027, brings together gearbox assembly, testing and painting under one roof. The unified design will streamline operations by reducing material handling steps and maximizing production flow. In addition, a dedicated warehouse will support efficient inbound and outbound logistics for components from suppliers and from Katsa’s nearby Tampere manufacturing plant and provide on-site storage. Katsas growth is driven by demand from multiple industries, including defense, industrial power generation and heavy equipment. While Katsa does not supply gearboxes directly to data centers, it provides components to major engine manufacturers who design and install backup power systems for these facilities. The company is currently adding 40 employees at its manufacturing operations and its two existing assembly locations in Tampere and will transition 25 experienced workers to the new facility in Pirkkala. By June 2027, Katsa expects to have a total workforce of approximately 250 employees. The site will feature a new 20-ton overhead crane-doubling the lifting capacity of Katsa's current assembly operation-and will enable the company to assemble and test larger industrial gearboxes. The facility will also include a renewable energy heating and cooling system. Ten geothermal wells, each about 1,150 feet deep, will provide approximately 98% of the building's heating and cooling needs. Construction recently reached a major milestone with the completion of the building's roof. To celebrate, Katsa hosted a traditional Finnish harjakaiset (topping off) ceremony.

articles.title: ClassNK endorses CYTUR shipboard cybersecurity management platform
articles.summary: ClassNK has granted its Innovation Endorsement for Products & Solutions to CYTUR-SBOM, a cybersecurity management platform developed by CYTUR for shipboard computer-based systems. The platform allows shipping companies to centrally manage information about onboard hardware, software, firmware and system...
articles.body: ClassNK has granted its Innovation Endorsement for Products & Solutions to CYTUR-SBOM, a cybersecurity management platform developed by CYTUR for shipboard computer-based systems. The platform allows shipping companies to centrally manage information about onboard hardware, software, firmware and system configurations. It also helps operators identify known cybersecurity vulnerabilities and monitor the security status of connected equipment. The endorsement forms part of ClassNK’s programme to support innovative maritime technologies through independent technical assessment. Platform supports onboard cybersecurity monitoring CYTUR-SBOM is a web-based platform designed to provide a structured inventory of computer-based systems installed on vessels. It records hardware, software and firmware information while providing visibility into the ship’s network topology. In addition, the platform assesses individual assets against security capability checklists. The results are recorded alongside supporting evidence, allowing operators to maintain a documented overview of their systems. CYTUR-SBOM also uses standardised product identifiers to compare registered equipment against the National Vulnerability Database maintained by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology. Through this process, the system can identify publicly recorded cybersecurity vulnerabilities associated with onboard equipment and software. Furthermore, the platform retains security assessment results, vulnerability identification records and document generation histories. Access is managed through defined user roles, with separate reading and writing permissions. The platform can also operate alongside CYTUR’s SC-P portable network scanner, which identifies computer-based systems by scanning a vessel’s onboard network. Endorsement has defined certification scope ClassNK granted the endorsement under its Innovation Endorsement for Products & Solutions programme, which evaluates technologies with innovative functions. However, the classification society clarified that the endorsement does not cover Chapters 4 and 5 of Part X of its Rules for the Survey and Construction of Steel Ships. It also does not certify compliance with IACS Unified Requirements UR E26 Rev.1 and UR E27 Rev.1. Therefore, the endorsement should not be interpreted as confirmation that the platform meets all applicable shipboard cyber resilience requirements. The recognition highlights the platform’s cybersecurity management capabilities, particularly its approach to asset inventories, network visibility and known vulnerability identification. The announcement did not provide details on commercial deployment, the number of vessels using the platform or any associated contract value.

articles.summary: Maritime experts warn that the westward spread of attacks between Russia and Ukraine, toward NATO coastlines, is now having commercial consequences.

REUTERS/ By Lori-Ann LaRocco – Maritime experts warn that the westward spread of attacks between Russia and Ukraine, toward NATO coastlines, is now having commercial consequences. “The sinking of Contship Jet off Bulgaria last week has crystallized those concerns,” said Richard Meade, editor-in-chief of Lloyd’s List. “We understand that analysts are being approached over potential charter-party disputes, as some owners are essentially seeking to refuse orders to Romanian and Bulgarian ports. That suggests to me that the calculation is shifting from how much the risk costs to whether owners, charterers and crews are prepared to accept it at all.” A series of drone attacks on vessels off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria has heightened concerns about maritime risk. In a Lloyd’s List briefing, Ambrey, a global maritime security, risk management and offshore support company, said it has recorded 696 security events in the Western Black Sea alone, about 537 of them in Ukrainian waters. “From July onwards, the cadence of the operations by both Russia and Ukraine has been unprecedented,” said Tomas Alexa, senior analyst at Ambrey. “With the start of Operation MoLoChKa, we have seen a significant rise in the number of attacks.” That includes direct attacks on merchant vessels in Romanian, Bulgarian, Turkish and Georgian waters. All three countries are members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO). “We have observed a significant increase in the number of strikes by Russian forces as well, whether it is against ports in Ukraine or merchant vessels; we are now observing the geographical spread of these attacks,” Alexa said. “Therefore, all vessels operating in the Western Black Sea are now facing heightened threat and greater exposure.” Between Oct. 5 and Oct. 28, Ambrey recorded 10 strikes on ships at sea: eight by aerial drones and two by uncrewed surface vessels. All were attributed to Russia. Alexa said Ambrey still assesses the threat of direct strikes on vessels with no link to Ukraine from negligible to low. Separately, it raised the risk of vessels conducting search-and-rescue operations from low to moderate. “Overall, there is a heightened risk to all vessels across the Western Black Sea at the moment,” Alexa said. He said vessels taking part in rescues face the risk of secondary strikes and secondary explosions. “This can increase the risk of collateral damage,” he said. Operating close to a vessel that has been hit, or being misidentified, could also make a rescue vessel a target. Ambrey considers a vessel to fit the targeting profile if its owner, manager, charterer, cargo, or last or next port of call has a Ukrainian link. Alexa said the attack on the Liberian-flagged, Greek-owned Contship Jet off Bulgaria shows that cargo possibly bound for Ukraine may be enough to make a ship a target. The firm is still investigating whether the vessel carried dual-use cargo that would eventually have been delivered to a Ukrainian port. Russia has described Ukraine-bound cargo ships as carrying military or dual-use cargo. Ambrey said it has seen no evidence of this on any vessel struck in Romanian or Bulgarian waters. “While the attacks against vessels in Romania are not something new, they were very sporadic and rare,” Alexa said. “The majority of them took place off the coast of Sulina, where vessels were waiting for transits to Ukrainian waters, the Danube River Delta or the seaports.” Russia’s attacks on Ukrainian ports and infrastructure have cut Ukraine’s ability to export from its seaports by up to 95%, according to Ambrey data. The attacks have shifted Ukrainian grain exports, and Ambrey has tracked a significant push toward Sulina and the Danube River Delta ports. “We’ve been able to link nine out of the 10 vessels that have been attacked in Romanian and Bulgarian waters to Ukrainian trade,” Alexa said. “Whilst there is a greater geographical spread of attacks against merchant vessels into Romanian and Bulgarian waters, the Russian intent remains the same. It is to degrade the capability of Ukrainian authorities or Ukraine itself to import and export cargo, and that assessment stands.” Owners and crews reassess The expansion of attacks has led a number of owners and operators to contact Ambrey. Alexa said that over the past two years, risk assessments were largely for Ukrainian ports, Russian ports and eastern Turkey, where a number of vessels bound for Russia had been attacked. “There definitely is a significant escalation and change in threat perception,” Alexa said. “We now definitely see a heightened number of requirements for assessments for Romanian and Bulgarian ports and western Turkey, which was previously not the case. We are also aware that a number of crew members, masters, are now also reluctant to sail to Romania or Bulgaria. So that definitely is a heightened threat perception, and it is justified.” International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF) has said Russia’s war on Ukraine is the deadliest for seafarers since World War II. Grain backs up In August, the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Foreign Agricultural Service office in Kyiv cut its forecast for Ukraine’s grain exports, citing the deteriorating security situation in the Black Sea. The FAS forecasts that Ukraine’s ending stocks of wheat, corn and barley will roughly quadruple in the 2026/27 marketing year, to almost 25 million metric tons. Production of the three grains is expected to be the highest since 2021/22, the season in which the war began. The office said Ukraine’s storage capacity should allow farmers to hold large stocks. Ukraine’s agriculture minister has warned that if disruptions continue, they may need 10 to 12 million metric tons of additional temporary storage. Russia and Ukraine together account for about 27% of global wheat exports. The increase in attacks has sent wheat futures on the Chicago Board of Trade to their highest level since 2023, up 20% in the first nine months of the year. No deal in sight Alexa said Ambrey has assessed that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, and his team are reaching out to Turkish and Indian operators, as well as the Indian government, to re-establish the grain corridor or propose a halt to hostilities across the Black Sea. “However, at this point, the Russian conditions are not being met,” Alexa said. “The Kremlin is asking for not only cessation of strikes against grain vessels, but across all the energy infrastructure. Plus, they’re putting forward additional requirements.” Alexa warned Russia sees the degrading of Ukrainian exports as a win from an economic battle standpoint. Given the pace of Russian attacks, Ambrey expects the situation to continue for the next couple of months. While Ukrainian attacks have slowed, Ambrey warned they could pick up again if Russia does not stop its attacks. “As always with Russia and Ukraine, until everything is agreed, nothing is agreed,” Alexa said. articles.summary: Arsenio Dominguez is set to remain at the helm of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) until the end of 2031 after the UN shipping agency’s Council backed his appointment for another four-year term. articles.body: Operations Regulatory Dominguez gets nod for second term at IMO helm Adis Ajdin November 6, 2026 0 378 1 minute read IMO IMO Arsenio Dominguez is set to remain at the helm of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) until the end of 2031 after the UN shipping agency’s Council backed his appointment for another four-year term. The 40-member Council endorsed the Panamanian’s extension during its 138th session in London, with the decision still requiring formal approval from the IMO Assembly when it meets in late 2027. If approved, Dominguez will serve a second term from January 1, 2028, to December 31, 2031, extending his leadership of the world’s maritime regulator during a period of mounting challenges over shipping decarbonisation and maritime security. Dominguez, who took office in January 2024, has spent much of his first term navigating increasingly divided positions among member states over the IMO’s Net-Zero Framework, which aims to introduce a global marine fuel standard and emissions pricing mechanism. The framework, agreed in principle in April 2025, suffered a major setback last October when governments voted to delay its adoption by a year following strong opposition led by the United States and Saudi Arabia. Efforts to revive the agreement have continued throughout 2026, with negotiations set to culminate in another critical round of talks later this month. The Marine Environment Protection Committee meets from November 30 to December 3, followed by a planned extraordinary session on December 4 to revisit the framework’s adoption. The IMO has also faced mounting pressure over the safety of commercial shipping amid continuing attacks and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, Red Sea and Black Sea, issues that feature on the agenda of this week’s Council meeting. Dominguez, the IMO’s tenth secretary-general, previously served as director of its Marine Environment Division, administrative director and chief of staff. He also represented Panama at the organisation and chaired its Marine Environment Protection Committee. He succeeded South Korea’s Kitack Lim in January 2024 after securing the Council’s backing in July 2023 and subsequent Assembly approval.
