articles.title: India joins ISF Verify initiative for digital seafarer certification
articles.summary: India has joined the ISF Verify initiative, marking a significant step towards the wider adoption of digital seafarer certification across the global shipping industry. The agreement brings together India’s Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA), the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) and Lloyd’s...
articles.body: India has joined the ISF Verify initiative, marking a significant step towards the wider adoption of digital seafarer certification across the global shipping industry. The agreement brings together India’s Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA), the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) and Lloyd’s Register OneOcean (LROO). India supplies approximately 312,000 seafarers, making it the world’s second-largest seafarer supply country, according to the ICS/BIMCO Seafarer Workforce Report 2026. Together with the Philippines, which previously participated in the initiative, the two countries account for approximately 30% of the global seafarer workforce of 2.57 million. However, this figure represents the workforce covered by the participating countries, rather than the number of seafarers already using the platform. The Memorandum of Understanding was signed during a meeting of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) Council in London. Pilot to explore integration with India’s certification system Under the agreement, the three organisations will undertake a pilot programme to explore connecting India’s existing certification platform with ISF Verify through an application programming interface (API). The initial phase will involve technical assessments, the identification of system requirements and the development of an integration roadmap. If the integration is successful, Indian seafarers will be able to synchronise certificates issued by their national maritime administration with ISF Verify. The cloud-based platform is designed to support the transition from paper certificates to secure digital verification. It connects seafarers, maritime administrations, shipping companies and port state control authorities, allowing certification information to be shared and checked more efficiently. Importantly, original certificates remain under the control and jurisdiction of the issuing authority. Seafarers also retain control over who can access their information. The system aims to reduce administrative work, support faster certificate endorsements and limit the risk of fraudulent documentation. It could also help reduce verification times during port inspections and crew-related administrative procedures. India strengthens international reach of ISF Verify India’s participation follows an earlier proof of concept involving the Philippines’ Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA). The addition of another major seafarer supply country expands the initiative’s potential international reach. Thomas A. Kazakos, Secretary General of ICS, said India’s involvement demonstrated growing confidence in a digital certification model that combines international connectivity with national control of data. Sushil Khopde, Additional Director General of Maritime Administration in India, highlighted the potential to improve seafarer mobility and simplify certification procedures while maintaining national oversight. Meanwhile, Andy McKeran, Chief Growth Officer at Lloyd’s Register and Managing Director of Lloyd’s Register OneOcean, described the agreement as an important step towards wider adoption of trusted digital certification. The partners have not announced a date for full operational integration in India. For now, the agreement establishes the framework for technical development and testing, rather than confirming that Indian seafarer certificates are already connected to ISF Verify. Successful implementation could provide a further step towards more consistent digital certificate verification across international shipping.

November 5, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Travel man The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA), the Research Council of Norway (RCN) and the Singapore Maritime Institute (SMI) have launched a joint research grant call to develop solutions to support the decarbonization of international shipping. The joint grant call brings together the research, technology and industry capabilities of Singapore’s and Norway’s maritime innovation ecosystems to address shared technological and operational challenges and develop solutions applicable across international shipping. The grant call builds on the MPA-RCN Memorandum of Understanding signed in April 2024 on maritime research, development, education and training. The grant call will focus on three areas: Alternative fuels and energy infrastructure: Improving the safety and handling of alternative marine fuels, developing bunkering and fuel storage technologies, and advancing charging infrastructure for electric vessels. Vessel energy efficiency and emissions reduction: Developing technologies to improve vessel performance, optimize onboard energy consumption and reduce fuel use. Digitalization and greener shipping operations: Advancing voyage optimization, just-in-time arrivals, autonomous operations and ship-port data exchange to improve operational efficiency and reduce emissions. SMI will provide up to USD$2.1 million (S$2.7 million) for Singapore research partners, while RCN will make available up to USD$2.15 million (NOK 20 million) for Norwegian research partners. Each proposal must involve research institutions and industry partners from both countries to ensure that the research addresses practical industry needs. Selected projects may receive funding for up to four years. This is the third Singapore–Norway joint research grant call, following earlier calls in 2015 and 2018 which supported four research projects in maritime energy efficiency, emissions reduction and emerging technologies. articles.body: Ukraine Renews Attacks on Russian Oil Refineries Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 5, 2026 © Adobe Stock/GoAerials Ukraine's renewed attacks on Russian oil refineries add to Moscow's difficulty in addressing domestic fuel shortages while it ships diesel to international markets under an export deal with US President Donald Trump. The Ryazan oil refinery, one of Russia's largest, appeared to have come under attack as part of a large drone strike overnight on industrial sites in the city, southeast of Moscow, according to a Reuters video analysis. If confirmed, it would be the second refinery to be hit this week following an attack on the Yaroslavl plant, northeast of Moscow, overnight on Monday, marking the breakdown of a pause in strikes. Ukraine's strikes on oil refineries this year forced large amounts of processing capacity in western Russia offline, causing fuel shortages that meant Moscow had to enforce fuel export bans from April onwards. A ban on diesel exports has been lifted in part and the US struck the deal in October with the Kremlin to resume diesel exports to international markets when Trump was seeking to calm diesel prices ahead of the midterm elections on November 3, which Trump's Republican Party lost. The city of Ryazan had restored power supply earlier on Thursday as fires at the unnamed industrial sites were either contained or put out, the local governor said on social media. US-RUSSIA DIESEL CARGOES ARE IN FOCUS At least six Russian diesel cargoes have broadcast that they plan transatlantic voyages, shipping data from Kpler and LSEG show, while two cargoes appeared to have changed course after being previously bound for the US Atlantic coast. No Russian diesel cargo has arrived in the US since the deal, the data show. The first observed US-bound Russian shipment is expected to arrive in New York this weekend, but regulatory, legislative and sanctions concerns mean that its discharge is not guaranteed, Kpler analyst Matt Smith said. "These are commercial loadings, so naturally the details cannot be made public. All the diesel will find its buyers," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on a daily conference call. Tankers often broadcast messages known as signals, such as "ATLANTIC COAST FOR ORDERS," indicating they are heading for the US Atlantic coast but have no confirmed discharge port, so the crew is awaiting instructions. Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Russian diesel cargoes destined for the US are continuing on course, in a post on X. There is no connection between diesel tankers changing course and the result of the US midterm elections, Peskov added. (Reuters)

articles.title: French Maritime Patrol Plane Extends Stay After Black Sea Cargo Vessel Attacks
articles.summary: A French maritime patrol aircraft deployed to Romania to bolster surveillance after a series of deadly strikes on merchant ships in the Black Sea on the edge of NATO's eastern flank will extend its stay by several weeks, its commander said on…
articles.body: French Maritime Patrol Plane Extends Stay After Black Sea Cargo Vessel Attacks Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 5, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Peter Hermes Furian A French maritime patrol aircraft deployed to Romania to bolster surveillance after a series of deadly strikes on merchant ships in the Black Sea on the edge of NATO's eastern flank will extend its stay by several weeks, its commander said on Thursday. The attacks have shown how the escalating maritime war between Russia and Ukraine is expanding into a major challenge for NATO in the Black Sea that has left member states such as Romania and Bulgaria exposed. The Black Sea is crucial for shipments of grain, oil and oil products and is shared by Bulgaria, Romania, Georgia and Turkey, as well as Ukraine and Russia. Russia has denied targeting Ukraine's neighbours. France temporarily relocated the Atlantique 2 aircraft — designed to detect submarines, warships and small threats including sea drones and mines — to the Romanian Mihail Kogalniceanu air base on October 18 after NATO members Romania and Bulgaria asked NATO for reinforcements. "The Atlantique 2 presence will be maintained for a few weeks from now on. We are here to ensure the safety of navigation of the commercial traffic in the Black Sea," said the aircraft's commander, whose identity was not given by the French naval forces for security purposes. It had initially been deployed to Romania until November 6. At least nine cargo ships were hit near the coast of Romania and Bulgaria in October, with some 34 sailors reported dead or missing. The plane was able to detect the three sea drones which ultimately struck and sank the Greek-owned container vessel Contship Jet in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone on October 28. The commander said they notified Bulgarian authorities and the vessel an hour before the sea drones struck, enabling the crew in that instance to come away unscathed. "We are a surveillance aircraft," the plane's commander said. "We are able to detect. We are not able to neutralise and intercept these kind of drones." NATO said this week the alliance had committed to investing more than $40 billion in counter-drone capabilities in the next five years. It said its commitment to defending all its members, including those on the Black Sea, was "ironclad". (Reuters)

November 5, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Faraways Iran reported three more tankers had been damaged in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, making clear that shipping would remain in peril as long as the war in the Gulf is unresolved, now that US voters have punished President Donald Trump for waging it. The electoral rout that cost Trump's Republicans control of Congress has prompted a stark reassessment of the conflict's political cost in Washington, led by Vice President JD Vance, who said in a long social media post on Wednesday that the war was to blame for his party's defeat. In a mocking reply on Thursday, Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, Vance's opposite number at previous peace talks, accused Vance of letting Trump double down like a "losing gambler" by planning more US strikes. If Vance believed the war was a mistake he should persuade Trump to call it off, Qalibaf said: "Skip the TED talk. Why not say this to your boss?" Oil prices have plunged in recent days as traders wagered that Trump, chastened by voters, may be less likely to restart the strikes he launched alongside Israel as "Operation Epic Fury" in February. Prices bounced back slightly on Thursday but are down more than $20 a barrel from last week. Iranian officials have been meeting with Qatari mediators since last week to discuss proposals to end the hostilities. But neither side has announced any breakthroughs on the major issues that have prevented any peace agreement so far. ATTACKS ON TANKERS AT RECORD PACE Meanwhile, attacks on tankers in the Gulf are still running close to a record pace. At least five vessels have reported incidents since Sunday, according to UK maritime security agency UKMTO, around the same rate as in October when the agency said 35 vessels were hit, the most of any month of the war. The UKMTO reported that a vessel had been struck by two unidentified projectiles late on Wednesday. Iran's Revolutionary Guards, who do not typically acknowledge firing on merchant ships but say the transit route is unsafe without Tehran's consent, said two tankers had struck naval mines and another had caught fire on Thursday. On Wednesday Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei said there should not be "even the slightest inclination towards submission" to the United States, which he said would remain hostile towards Iran no matter which party was in power. 'HE IS PLANNING TO BOMB IRAN' When asked about Vance's comments on the war on Wednesday, Trump defended the decision to launch it, saying it was important to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, a justification he has repeatedly cited. A White House adviser told Reuters that some officials and staff inside the White House viewed Vance's post as a foreign policy break from the president and a public recognition of the war's economic consequences. But two sources told Reuters they believed Trump was still likely to order resumed hostilities. "He is planning to bomb Iran. Don’t listen to what he’s saying. He held off because of the midterms. We asked him to hold off until the midterms," said one of the sources. The other said Trump did not have anything to lose politically now ⁠that the midterms were over. Peacemaking efforts have revolved around the future status of the strait, a US blockade on Iranian ports, sanctions on the Islamic Republic and a resumption of negotiations over Tehran's nuclear programme. A senior Iranian official said this week that the two sides remain far apart. Qatar said on Tuesday that the United States and Iran were committed to mediation efforts and were reviewing proposals aimed at bridging their differences, adding that there had been developments in talks with both sides. (Reuters)

articles.title: Brazilian builds boat from rubbish to collect more rubbish
articles.summary: A former Brazilian ocean canoeing champion has taken recycling to a floating extreme, constructing a boat from 230 discarded plastic containers so he can collect even more rubbish from the sea. Marcos Arnhold spent two months building the unusual craft in Guaratuba, southern Brazil, using 125 two-litre plastic...
articles.body: Americas Environment Brazilian builds boat from rubbish to collect more rubbish Sam Chambers November 6, 2026 0 4,905 1 minute read A former Brazilian ocean canoeing champion has taken recycling to a floating extreme, constructing a boat from 230 discarded plastic containers so he can collect even more rubbish from the sea. Marcos Arnhold spent two months building the unusual craft in Guaratuba, southern Brazil, using 125 two-litre plastic bottles, 105 five-litre disinfectant containers and a metal roof rack salvaged from an old Volkswagen Kombi. The homemade vessel is destined for Guaratuba Bay and its surrounding mangroves, where Arnhold plans to collect discarded rubbish for delivery to a municipal recycling centre. The former athlete, who won Brazil’s national ocean canoeing championship in 2002, told local newspaper JB Litoral that initial flotation and stability tests have exceeded expectations. The vessel currently has a 6.5 hp petrol engine, although Arnhold hopes eventually to add a sail and switch to electric propulsion. Friends donated bottles, while local sponsors helped finance the engine and trailer. Applauding the initiative, Graeme Somerville-Ryan, the founder of Eyesea, told Splash: “Never underestimate the endeavor, endurance, and effort of good people wanting to change the world. He should be celebrated and supported. But we know ocean and coastal pollution is an industrial-sized problem, and we need industrial solutions. This is where shipping and maritime people can, and are, making a difference.” Eyesea is a maritime environmental non-profit that uses crowdsourced photographs, geolocation data and satellite technology to map marine pollution and help coordinate targeted clean-up efforts worldwide. articles.body: Navios Maritime Partners reported a sharp rise in third-quarter earnings as the shipowner expanded its containership orderbook and secured additional long-term charter revenue. The company generated revenue of US$432 million during the third quarter of 2026, up 24.5% from US$346.9 million in the same period last year. Net income more than tripled to US$185.7 million from US$56.3 million. Adjusted net income reached US$163.7 million, compared with US$83.7 million a year earlier. For the first nine months of 2026, revenue increased by 22.5% to US$1.2 billion. Net income rose to US$459.9 million from US$168 million. “For the third quarter, we reported net income of US$185.7 million and earnings per common unit of US$6.42,” said Angeliki Frangou, chairwoman and chief executive officer of Navios Partners. “Our financial and operating performance demonstrates the strength of our diversified business and the benefits of our disciplined approach to capital allocation and risk management,” she added. Four 10,100 TEU newbuildings In September, Navios Partners agreed to acquire four new 10,100 TEU containerships for a combined US$488 million. The scrubber-equipped ships will also feature shore-power connections. Deliveries are scheduled between the second half of 2028 and the first half of 2029. All four vessels have already secured charters lasting approximately 5.6 years. They will earn an average net daily rate of US$48,263. The company also took delivery of a methanol-ready and scrubber-fitted 7,900 TEU containership in September. The vessel has been chartered for approximately four years at a net rate of US$42,463 per day. Navios Partners now has ten containership newbuildings scheduled for delivery through the first half of 2029. Its orderbook comprises two 7,900 TEU ships, four 8,850 TEU vessels and four 10,100 TEU units. Charter backlog reaches US$5 billion Navios Partners secured US$735.1 million of additional contracted revenue across its containership, tanker and dry bulk fleets. Eight containerships were fixed for an average period of 4.2 years at an average net rate of US$43,457 per day. Following these agreements, the company’s total contracted revenue stands at US$5 billion, extending through 2037. Navios Partners’ fleet includes 54 containerships, alongside 65 dry bulk vessels and 63 tankers. The total excludes one 4,730 TEU boxship that the company has agreed to sell. The containership fleet generated an average time charter equivalent rate of US$31,619 per day during the third quarter. This was slightly below the US$31,832 reported a year earlier. Overall fleet utilisation reached 99.3%, while the combined daily time charter equivalent rate increased by 25.7% to US$30,371.

Join the leading maritime news network IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez at the opening of the IMO Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) 2nd extraordinary session, 14-17 October, 2025. Photo courtesy IMO The International Maritime Organization (IMO) Council has backed Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez for a second four-year term, extending its support for his leadership despite the organization’s failure to adopt its landmark Net-Zero Framework and an escalating security crisis threatening commercial shipping. The decision, announced Wednesday during the Council’s 138th session in London, would extend Dominguez’s mandate from January 1, 2028, through December 31, 2031, subject to formal approval by the IMO Assembly in late 2027. “I am deeply grateful to the Members of the Council and all Members of the Organization for their continued trust and support,” Dominguez said in an IMO statement . The endorsement comes at a particularly challenging time for the UN maritime agency, which has struggled to build consensus on climate regulations while confronting mounting threats to freedom of navigation and the safety of seafarers. Dominguez presided over a major setback in October 2025, when IMO member states failed to formally adopt the organization’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, a landmark package of global fuel standards and greenhouse gas emissions pricing measures for international shipping, amid pressure from the United States and other oil-producing countries. Although the framework had secured initial approval in April 2025, divisions among member states ultimately derailed its adoption. Delegates voted to adjourn the extraordinary Marine Environment Protection Committee session for one year, leaving the proposed regulations in limbo. The outcome represented a significant blow to years of international negotiations aimed at establishing a global regulatory framework for shipping’s transition away from fossil fuels. The United States and several oil-producing countries strongly opposed the proposal, particularly its emissions-pricing mechanism, while supporters argued that globally coordinated regulations were essential to reducing shipping emissions and avoiding a patchwork of competing regional requirements. Dominguez defended the process following the setback, maintaining that the framework remained alive despite the failure to secure its adoption. A year later, the divisions remain unresolved. Negotiators are scheduled to reconvene later this month ahead of the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s 85th session, November 30 to December 3. A special session to consider adoption of the framework is provisionally scheduled for December 4. The latest round of negotiations will be another major test of the IMO’s ability to reconcile competing national interests. Meanwhile, the organization faces an increasingly dangerous security environment for commercial shipping. According to the IMO’s latest figures , 129 maritime incidents have been confirmed in the Strait of Hormuz and wider Middle East since the Iran war began in February, with 24 seafarers killed as of November 5. The tally includes vessels damaged, sunk or detained, underscoring the continued dangers facing civilian shipping in one of the world’s most strategically important maritime regions. The escalating crisis has raised fundamental questions about freedom of navigation and the international community’s ability to protect merchant ships and innocent seafarers caught in armed conflicts. Opening this week’s Council meeting, Dominguez again condemned the threats facing commercial shipping in the Middle East and other conflict zones, including the Red Sea and Black Sea. But while the IMO has repeatedly called for the protection of seafarers and the restoration of safe navigation, its ability to influence the underlying military and geopolitical conflicts remains limited. The simultaneous challenges have placed the organization in an increasingly difficult position, with geopolitical divisions complicating both its environmental agenda and its longstanding mandate to promote safe and secure international shipping. A Panamanian naval architect and longtime maritime diplomat, Dominguez became the IMO’s tenth Secretary-General on January 1, 2024, succeeding Kitack Lim. He previously served as director of the organization’s Marine Environment Division and held several senior diplomatic and administrative positions. The Council’s endorsement signals continued confidence in Dominguez despite the setbacks, leaving him positioned to lead the IMO through a period of mounting pressure on the international regulatory system governing commercial shipping. articles.title: Tender-Assist Rigs: Southeast Asia’s Quiet Workhorses Head for Full Utilization
articles.summary: Often overshadowed by the towering jackup and ultra-deepwater floating rig fleets that dominate offshore headlines, tender-assist rigs are enjoying a resurgence in Southeast Asia. While they represent a relatively small niche of the global offshore drilling market…
articles.body: Tender-Assist Rigs: Southeast Asia’s Quiet Workhorses Head for Full Utilization Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. By Paul Ezekiel, Senior Offshore Rig Analyst, Westwood Global Energy Group November 5, 2026 EDrill-2 tender-assist drilling rig © Energy Drilling About the Author: Paul Ezekiel joined Westwood Global Energy Group in August 2018 as an Offshore Rig Analyst. He has more than 28 years in the offshore industry focused on Marketing, Contracts and Business Development. He has served as Chartering Manager at Seacor Marine and Commercial Manager at Tidewater International. Ezekiel holds a Master Mariner Class I Licence from the Australian Maritime College and an MBA from the University of Hull. He has also spent time as a Senior Lecturer at the Si Often overshadowed by the towering jackup and ultra-deepwater floating rig fleets that dominate offshore headlines, tender-assist rigs are enjoying a resurgence in Southeast Asia. While they represent a relatively small niche of the global offshore drilling market, these versatile units have become indispensable to operators across Thailand, Malaysia and Brunei, where their efficiency and cost competitiveness continue to drive demand. Tender-assist rigs are designed for fast, efficient platform drilling. Conventional units use a barge-like monohull and are best suited to shallow, calm waters, while larger semi-tenders can operate in deeper and more challenging environments such as offshore East Malaysia and the Andaman Sea. The key attraction is speed. Compared with jackups, tender-assist rigs require less time to mobilize, rig up and move between locations. In some cases, drilling equipment can be installed in as few as three lifts, reducing non-productive time and improving well economics. A Market Concentrated in Southeast Asia According to Westwood's RigLogix, the global fleet comprises of just 29 tender-assist and semi tender-assist rigs (collectively referred to here as TARs). Of these, 16 are currently active, six are warm stacked, six are cold stacked and one remains under construction. Yet despite their modest numbers, the market is tightening rapidly, with Southeast Asia standing as the only region where the sector is truly thriving. Figure 1: Average Age of Global Tender-Assist Rig Fleet © Westwood RigLogix Not only are rigs actively drilling throughout the Asia Pacific region, but there has also been recent reactivation activity, new construction and visible demand for upcoming well programs. Outside this region, the picture is markedly different. Idle units are scattered across locations including China, Greece, Venezuela, Romania and Spain, with many having been inactive for years. In contrast, operators across Malaysia and Thailand continue to rely heavily on TARs to support development drilling campaigns on established offshore platforms. A Market Dominated by Two Players The Southeast Asian TAR market remains highly concentrated. The primary fleet owners are Vantris Energy, formerly part of Sapura Energy, and Energy Drilling, which together control most of the operational units available in the region. Elsewhere, PetroVietnam Drilling manages a single semi-tender currently working for Shell Brunei on a long-term contract, while Keppel's Raiqa TAR remains under construction. The limited availability of rigs means contracts are frequently awarded through direct negotiations or restricted tenders rather than fully competitive bidding rounds. PTTEP Leads Demand Thailand's national oil company PTTEP is currently the world's largest user of TARs. The company has eight tender-assist units and two semi-tenders under contract, with one of the latter operating in Myanmar. PTTEP's extensive platform infrastructure in the Gulf of Thailand is ideally suited to these units. The region's shallow water depths and relatively calm sea conditions make TARs a natural fit, although recent tenders indicate the operator is increasingly willing to consider either TARs or jackups depending on program requirements. Further demand comes from Carigali-PTTEP Operating Company (CPOC), which currently has a semi-tender working in the Malaysia-Thailand Joint Development Area. Malaysia remains another cornerstone of regional demand. PETRONAS Carigali currently has three TARs under contract, while operators including EnQuest, Vestigo, Shell, JX Nippon, ConocoPhillips and PTTEP Sabah continue to utilise these units across the country's offshore fields. Historically, ExxonMobil was a major user of TARs in the Palas and Dulang fields before operatorship transferred to PETRONAS Carigali. This broad operator base has helped support a consistently healthy domestic market and provided stability for fleet owners, even during broader offshore industry downturns. A Tightening Market Fleet utilization has already reached approximately 96%, and the market appears poised to tighten further. Excluding the cold-stacked T-9 and the newbuild Raiqa, effective utilisation is expected to reach 100% before the end of the fourth quarter. Looking ahead, 2027 promises to be particularly active for semi-tenders in Malaysia. Major drilling campaigns are scheduled to begin from March onwards, including Shell's Malikai Phase 3 programme, PTTEP's Kikeh Phase 3 development and ConocoPhillips' Kebabangan Cluster campaign. Activity is also expected to expand beyond Malaysia. Offshore Vietnam, the Bien Dong project is anticipated to generate additional demand beginning in the first quarter of 2028. Rates Rising Alongside Demand Historically, TARs have commanded dayrates slightly below those of jackups, reflecting their specialist role and more limited geographic market. Over the past 12 months, however, that gap has narrowed as utilization has tightened across Southeast Asia. Today, four TARs are securing rates above US$120,000 per day, underlining the strength of demand and the scarcity of available units. Asia Pacific Tender & Jackup Average Leading-Edge Dayrates 2021-2026 © Westwood RigLogix Contract durations vary across the fleet, ranging from short-term campaigns to multi-year agreements. PTTEP remains a notable exception, typically favoring long-term contracts to support its substantial production commitments in the Gulf of Thailand. For companies considering a newbuild TAR, historical benchmarks provide a useful starting point, although today's reality would likely involve longer delivery schedules and significantly higher construction costs. Historically, a unit could be built in around 24 months from order to delivery. Figure 3: Historical Tender-Assist Rig Newbuild Construction © Source Westwood RigLogix. Whether a newbuild is commercially viable depends on balancing the cost of investment against the relatively small size of the global TAR market. However, with utilization nearing full capacity, dayrates strengthening and limited newbuild activity in recent years, the sector appears increasingly exposed to a future supply shortage. Should demand continue to grow across Southeast Asia, contractors may find that fleet expansion becomes not only attractive but necessary to meet operator requirements.

REUTERS/Jon Nazca/File Photo A.P. Moller-Maersk is pressing ahead with one of its largest containership ordering programs in years, confirming in its third-quarter earnings report that it has ordered 26 LNG dual-fuel vessels with a combined capacity of nearly 484,000 TEU. The Danish shipping giant highlighted the orders in its 3rd quarter earnings release , marking another major commitment to fleet renewal as the industry continues investing in larger, more fuel-efficient ships. Each vessel will have a capacity of 18,600 TEU, with deliveries scheduled for 2029 and 2030. The order, first confirmed by Maersk in September, represents 483,600 TEU of newbuilding capacity, equivalent to roughly 10% of the carrier’s existing operating fleet. The company has not publicly disclosed the contract value or identified the shipyards involved. The orders follow a separate February agreement for eight 18,600-TEU containerships at New Times Shipbuilding in China, also scheduled for delivery in 2029 and 2030. That earlier series was designed with operational flexibility in mind. At 366 meters long and 58.6 meters wide, the vessels are smaller than the largest 24,000-TEU ships being built by competitors. “Deployment flexibility has been a key factor in our decision-making,” Anda Cristescu, Maersk’s Head of Chartering & Newbuilding, said when the February order was announced. The latest commitment also underscores Maersk’s growing embrace of LNG-capable propulsion after years in which the company was among the shipping industry’s most prominent advocates for methanol. Maersk began moving toward a broader fuel strategy in 2024, when it ordered 20 dual-fuel vessels totaling 300,000 TEU. Those ships were equipped with liquefied gas dual-fuel engines, marking a significant expansion beyond its earlier methanol-focused newbuilding program. The company has argued that shipping’s energy transition will require multiple fuel pathways rather than a single solution. LNG-capable engines can operate on conventional marine fuels or liquefied natural gas, while potentially allowing a transition to lower-emission alternatives such as bio-LNG as supplies develop. That flexibility is becoming increasingly important as shipowners face uncertainty over fuel availability, costs and future emissions regulations. As gCaptain reported this week , a new Lloyd’s Register study found that LNG bunkering was available at 222 ports worldwide, compared with just 25 ports offering methanol. The disparity helps explain why LNG continues to dominate alternative-fuel newbuilding orders despite questions about its long-term climate benefits. The surge in LNG orders also raises questions about future fleet capacity. While Maersk describes the latest contracts as part of its ongoing renewal program, the 26 ships represent a substantial addition to its construction pipeline at a time when major rivals including MSC, CMA CGM and COSCO are also investing heavily in new tonnage. Maersk has previously said its fleet renewal strategy is intended largely to replace older vessels rather than permanently expand overall capacity. The eventual impact on fleet size will therefore depend partly on how much existing tonnage is retired or returned to charter owners as the new ships enter service. The newbuilding commitment comes as Maersk’s Ocean business benefits from tight vessel availability, port congestion and higher freight rates. The company’s third-quarter operating profit rose sharply to $2.6 billion, up from $567 million a year earlier, with fleet utilization reaching 96%. For Maersk, the challenge is balancing those strong near-term market conditions against a newbuilding cycle that will bring substantial capacity into service toward the end of the decade. With the first of the 26 ships not expected until 2029, the orders are as much a bet on the shape of the container shipping market in the 2030s as they are an investment in the company’s next generation of vessels. articles.title: Matson raises outlook as China volumes climb 16%
articles.summary: Matson reported stronger third-quarter results and raised its full-year outlook, supported by higher volumes and freight rates on its China services. The US carrier generated consolidated revenue of US$1.11 billion during the third quarter of 2026. This represents an increase of 26.5% from US$880.1 million in the...
articles.body: Matson reported stronger third-quarter results and raised its full-year outlook, supported by higher volumes and freight rates on its China services. The US carrier generated consolidated revenue of US$1.11 billion during the third quarter of 2026. This represents an increase of 26.5% from US$880.1 million in the same period last year. Net income rose to US$209.4 million from US$134.7 million, while diluted earnings per share increased from US$4.24 to US$6.96. Consolidated operating income reached US$255.2 million, compared with US$161 million a year earlier. “Matson had a stronger-than-expected third quarter,” said Matt Cox, chairman and chief executive officer of Matson. “Our China service performed well, with its speed and reliability serving as important differentiators amid continued pressure on global shipping networks and congestion at key Asian ports,” he added. China volumes drive shipping growth Matson’s Ocean Transportation segment recorded revenue of US$891.3 million, up 24.1% year-on-year. Operating income increased by 62.2% to US$239.1 million. The company attributed the improvement primarily to higher freight rates and volumes on its China services. Increased fuel-related surcharge revenue also supported the result, although higher fuel costs raised vessel operating expenses. China service volumes, which include cargo from other Asian origins, increased by 16% to 40,500 FEUs. Matson said strong demand and elevated freight rates produced a substantial increase in the service’s contribution compared with the weaker 2025 peak season. The company expects these conditions to continue through the end of 2026 and into early 2027. Volumes on the Guam service increased by 4.3% to 4,800 FEUs. However, Hawaii volumes slipped by 0.3% to 36,200 FEUs, while Alaska volumes declined by 4.8% to 22,000 FEUs. Matson expects its full-year China and Guam volumes to exceed their 2025 levels. Hawaii and Alaska volumes are forecast to finish modestly lower. Logistics revenue rises Matson’s Logistics segment generated third-quarter revenue of US$222.2 million, an increase of 37.3% from the previous year. Operating income rose by 18.4% to US$16.1 million. Higher contributions from transportation brokerage and freight forwarding offset weaker warehousing performance. The company expects fourth-quarter Logistics operating income to be modestly higher than the US$7.7 million reported in the final quarter of 2025. Stronger fourth-quarter forecast Matson now expects Ocean Transportation operating income in the fourth quarter to be approximately 50% higher than the US$136 million recorded a year earlier. Consolidated operating income is also forecast to rise by around 50% from the fourth-quarter 2025 result of US$143.7 million. “Looking ahead, we expect the strong demand and elevated freight rates we experienced in our China service in the third quarter to continue through year-end and into early 2027,” noted Cox. Matson invested US$52.5 million in vessel construction during the quarter. It expects full-year vessel construction expenditure, including capitalised interest and owner-supplied items, to reach approximately US$375 million. The company also repurchased approximately 300,000 shares for US$59.8 million during the third quarter.

articles.body: Contracts & Tenders November 5, 2026 · 2 minutes ago Excelerate and AxDo strike multi-year Bahamas LNG deal for Caribbean’s new terminal Excelerate Energy and AxDo Bahamas have sealed an 11-year LNG supply agreement for a new offshore hub near Grand Bahama. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Source: Excelerate Energy Excelerate Energy, a U.S.-based liquefied natural gas (LNG) and power infrastructure firm headquartered in Texas, and AxDo Bahamas, a joint venture between Axpo and Domicisle LNG, have signed a long-term supply deal to anchor an offshore LNG storage and distribution terminal off Grand Bahama that aims to deliver up to 16 trillion British thermal units annually to strengthen energy security across the Bahamas and the wider Caribbean. Excelerate Energy and AxDo Bahamas have confirmed an 11-year LNG supply agreement supporting development of the Bahamas LNG hub, enabling the local firm to become an anchor customer of the U.S. player’s planned offshore LNG storage and distribution terminal near the island of Grand Bahama. " The Bahamas LNG Hub demonstrates the potential of our integrated platform to create new opportunities around our infrastructure. By combining LNG supply, logistics, and infrastructure with strong downstream partners, we can develop new markets and expand access to natural gas across the region. We’re pleased to partner with AxDo and look forward to supporting growing demand in the Bahamas and throughout the Caribbean. " — Oliver Simpson Executive Vice President and Chief Commercial Officer of Excelerate Energy This deal enables deliveries of up to 16 trillion British thermal units of LNG a year, establishing a long-term commercial foundation for the project. The combination of AxDo’s shipping and bunkering expertise with Excelerate’s LNG infrastructure and supply capabilities is intended to help meet growing LNG demand across The Bahamas and the broader Caribbean. " Reliable access to energy is essential for the continued development of The Bahamas and the wider Caribbean. Axpo brings extensive experience in energy markets and international supply chains. This agreement allows us to apply that know-how to the Caribbean, working with key partners Excelerate and Domicisle to support the development of a flexible LNG hub for The Bahamas and the wider region. " — Daniele Corti Axpo’s Head of Small-Scale LNG With initial LNG deliveries expected to begin in 2027 utilizing existing LNG supply and logistics capabilities from Excelerate’s Jamaica platform, a second phase is expected to include deployment of a floating storage unit (FSU) near Grand Bahama in 2028, subject to final permitting and construction timelines and other contractual provisions. This FSU will serve as the offshore LNG storage and distribution terminal. " This agreement represents an important step forward for the Bahamas and for the development of a reliable LNG supply network across our islands. As a Bahamian-based company, our focus is on making cleaner-burning natural gas more accessible to power producers, marine operators, and communities that need dependable energy. By combining Domicisle’s local market knowledge and distribution capabilities with Axpo’s international energy expertise and Excelerate’s LNG infrastructure, we are building a practical foundation for long-term energy security and economic growth in The Bahamas and the wider Caribbean. " — Greg Buffington Domicisle LNG’s Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Located in one of the Caribbean’s busiest maritime corridors, Excelerate believes that Grand Bahama is strategically positioned to support cruise ship bunkering, power generation, and regional LNG distribution demand while enhancing regional LNG logistics capabilities and energy security. The planned Bahamas LNG hub is designed to provide LNG storage and distribution services for marine bunkering, power generation, and other downstream customers while expanding access to natural gas across the region. articles.title: The Hidden Liabilities In Maritime Acquisitions
articles.summary: What Buyers, Sellers and Investors Often Miss During Due DiligenceBy Sabrina Brigance, CMIP, Managing Director, Marine Practice, Hylant Maritime mergers and acquisitions can create significant opportunities for growth. Private equity...

Join the leading maritime news network What Buyers, Sellers and Investors Often Miss During Due Diligence By Sabrina Brigance, CMIP, Managing Director, Marine Practice, Hylant Maritime mergers and acquisitions can create significant opportunities for growth. Private equity firms, strategic buyers and marine operators may pursue acquisitions to expand capabilities, add assets, enter new markets and strengthen their position across the maritime industry. But buying a marine business is not the same as buying a traditional operating company. Marine organizations combine vessels and waterfront assets with specialized labor, complex contracts, environmental exposures, regulatory requirements and increasingly connected technology. Those operating realities can materially affect the economics of an otherwise attractive transaction and are among the critical considerations explored in Hylant’s Maritime M&A Risk Guide . Financial diligence tells a buyer what a company earns. Marine risk diligence should help determine whether the assets and operations behind those earnings can sustain them. What Are You Really Acquiring? I refer to this as the Quality of Risk. Two marine companies may generate similar earnings yet carry vastly different levels of operational volatility, capital requirements and liability. One may operate well-maintained assets supported by disciplined safety and risk-management practices, while the other may face deferred maintenance, aging infrastructure, unresolved claims or significant workforce dependencies. Identifying these differences before closing is critical to understanding the risk behind the earnings. The Marine Assets Tell the Real Risk Story A vessel schedule may show ownership, age and value, but it does not necessarily reveal upcoming drydock requirements, machinery reliability, maintenance backlogs, casualty history or outstanding survey issues. The same principle applies to shoreside assets. Shipyard dry docks, cranes, fire protection systems and waterfront infrastructure can create significant operational and capital requirements. Terminals may depend on individual berths, cranes or other critical equipment. Deferred maintenance can function like hidden transaction debt. The expense may not appear in the purchase price, but the buyer can inherit the obligation. That is why physical asset diligence needs to go beyond the asset schedule. Insurance Programs Tell a Story Insurance due diligence should involve more than confirming that policies exist and limits appear adequate. Historical losses, open claims, reserves, deductibles, self-insured retentions and coverage gaps can provide insight into how the organization has managed risk over time. In a marine acquisition, I would go further: Does the insurance architecture actually match the operation? Are vessel values, navigation limits and P&I provisions appropriate? Are crew, longshore and state workers’ compensation exposures classified correctly? Do ship repair, terminal, stevedoring, pollution and cargo coverages accurately reflect the services the company provides? The important question is not simply whether insurance exists. It is whether the insurance program responds to the marine operation as it is actually performed. Environmental Liabilities Can Outlive Ownership Waterfront facilities, shipyards, terminals, fuel systems and vessel operations can create environmental exposures that require specialized diligence. Historical contamination, tanks, sediment and dredging issues, waste handling, stormwater, spill history, vessel pollution and operating permits may all warrant review. The buyer needs to understand not only whether a condition exists, but whether it could affect safe operations, vessel movement, dredging, fueling, permitting or continued use of the facility. The Human Capital Factor Is Uniquely Maritime Marine businesses depend heavily on specialized people. Licensed mariners, skilled tradespeople and experienced waterfront personnel can be difficult to replace. Workforce diligence should consider critical-role dependencies, succession, safety performance, labor considerations and employee classification. That classification issue is distinctly maritime. State workers’ compensation, USL&H and Jones Act exposures can intersect within the same organization. Understanding what employees actually do, where they work, and their connection to vessels is an important part of understanding that risk. Marine Contracts Can Shift the Risk Charters, ship repair contracts, terminal agreements, towing arrangements and customer contracts can determine who carries the financial consequences when something goes wrong. Indemnification, insurance requirements, limitations of liability and other risk-allocation provisions, which are examined more closely in Hylant’s Maritime M&A Risk Guide , should be evaluated alongside the company’s actual operations and insurance program. A profitable marine contract can still create significant exposure if the organization has accepted liabilities its operating controls or insurance cannot support. When Technology Failure Becomes Operational Downtime Cyber diligence should also consider the operational consequences of technology failure. What happens if a vessel navigation system, terminal platform, crane, berth or other critical asset becomes unavailable? Is substitute equipment or capacity available? How quickly can the operation recover? For marine buyers, technology risk increasingly needs to be considered alongside business interruption and operational resilience. When Marine Diligence Meets the Deal Representations and warranties insurance can play an important role in certain transactions, but it does not replace strong marine diligence. Once diligence identifies deferred maintenance, an environmental condition, a regulatory deficiency or another known exposure, the parties need to determine how to address the issue. Depending on the circumstances and advice of transaction counsel, that could involve remediation, contractual risk allocation, insurance or the economics of the transaction. The objective is not to turn every operational concern into an insurance issue. It is to understand the marine risk before ownership changes hands. Protecting the Value Created Risk management should not end when the deal closes. The first 100 days provide an opportunity to address outstanding maintenance and safety concerns, review open claims, validate asset schedules, align contractor practices, strengthen cyber controls and integrate insurance and risk-management programs. Maritime acquisitions create tremendous opportunities, but ultimately, the buyer is acquiring more than financial performance. The buyer is acquiring the operation behind those earnings. Understanding the vessels, waterfront assets, workforce, contracts, insurance, environmental exposures and technology supporting that operation can provide a much clearer picture of the risk being acquired. For a deeper look, download Hylant’s Maritime M&A Risk Guide: Identifying the Risks That Can Change Deal Value. articles.body: Production & Processing November 5, 2026 · 8 minutes ago After Subsea7, Aker BP contracts OneSubsea for Norwegian fast-track oil project NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email SLB OneSubsea Shortly after awarding Subsea7 a contract for the project, Aker BP has revealed that OneSubsea, a joint venture backed by SLB, Aker Solutions and Subsea7, has also been allocated work for the Lyra field development, formerly known as Kjøttkake, on the Norwegian Continental Shelf (NCS). Located in the northern part of the North Sea, approximately 44 kilometers from the Gjøa platform, the Lyra field will be tied back to the existing Gjøa platform through the NOVA field infrastructure. The OneSubsea joint venture has secured a contract to deliver subsea production systems, umbilicals and associated services for the field. According to SLB, Aker BP and OneSubsea worked together from the early stages of the project to shape the development strategy. "Our alliance with SLB OneSubsea, combined with standardized subsea technology, has been central to how we are developing Lyra,” said Marte Mogstad , Senior Vice President at Aker BP. “The project demonstrates how we together can make marginal resources economically viable through fast track execution, with three years from discovery to first oil." This comes a couple of days after it was reported that Subsea7 had secured an engineering, procurement, construction and installation (EPCI) contract for gas lift and production pipelines and associated subsea infrastructure for the field. The fast-track Lyra development is targeting first oil in 2028, three years after discovery. “Lyra shows what is possible with fast-track field development,” said Mads Hjelmeland , Chief Executive Officer of SLB OneSubsea. “Working together from the earliest stages allows us to shape development strategies around our customers’ priorities and create new opportunities for offshore resources.” Reach the Offshore Energy industry in one go! By Luiza Ilie MIHAIL KOGALNICEANU, Romania, Nov 5 (Reuters) – A French maritime patrol aircraft deployed to Romania to bolster surveillance after a series of deadly strikes on merchant ships in the Black Sea on the edge of NATO’s eastern flank will extend its stay by several weeks, its commander said on Thursday. The attacks have shown how the escalating maritime war between Russia and Ukraine is expanding into a major challenge for NATO in the Black Sea that has left member states such as Romania and Bulgaria exposed. The Black Sea is crucial for shipments of grain, oil and oil products and is shared by Bulgaria, Romania, Georgia and Turkey, as well as Ukraine and Russia. Russia has denied targeting Ukraine’s neighbors. France temporarily relocated the Atlantique 2 aircraft — designed to detect submarines, warships and small threats including sea drones and mines — to the Romanian Mihail Kogalniceanu air base on October 18 after NATO members Romania and Bulgaria asked NATO for reinforcements . “The Atlantique 2 presence will be maintained for a few weeks from now on. We are here to ensure the safety of navigation of the commercial traffic in the Black Sea,” said the aircraft’s commander, whose identity was not given by the French naval forces for security purposes. It had initially been deployed to Romania until November 6. At least nine cargo ships were hit near the coast of Romania and Bulgaria in October, with some 34 sailors reported dead or missing. The plane was able to detect the three sea drones which ultimately struck and sank the Greek-owned container vessel Contship Jet in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone on October 28. The commander said they notified Bulgarian authorities and the vessel an hour before the sea drones struck, enabling the crew in that instance to come away unscathed. “We are a surveillance aircraft,” the plane’s commander said. “We are able to detect. We are not able to neutralize and intercept these kind of drones.” NATO said this week the alliance had committed to investing more than $40 billion in counter-drone capabilities in the next five years. It said its commitment to defending all its members, including those on the Black Sea, was “ironclad.” (Reporting by Luiza Ilie;Editing by Alison Williams) (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026. articles.body: Decommissioning November 5, 2026 · 1 minute ago RINA to mobilize up to 83 experts for €11 million contract with Petrobras NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email RINA Inspection, certification and consulting engineering group RINA has signed a three-year €11 million contract with Brazilian oil & gas giant Petrobras to support initiatives related to the integrity and decommissioning of subsea systems. The scope covers studies and analyses focused on the integrity, reliability and maintenance of subsea systems, supporting the evaluation of different operational scenarios throughout their lifecycle. Key activities include integrity assessments of pipelines and risers, reliability studies, such as FMEA/FMECA and RAM, asset life extension evaluations, and the development of technical studies for subsea decommissioning projects. The contract further involves the mobilization of up to 83 professionals, including engineers and specialized technicians, around 45 of whom are part of RINA’s existing workforce. The team may be further expanded throughout the contract period to meet evolving project needs and requirements. According to RINA, the project is aligned with Petrobras’ initiatives aimed at ensuring the safe and efficient lifecycle management of its offshore assets. The objective is to support both the safe continuation of operations in active units and the responsible planning of interventions and decommissioning activities for structures that have reached the end of their operational lifecycle. “Projects related to the integrity and decommissioning of subsea systems require robust technical analysis and deep offshore engineering expertise. In this partnership with Petrobras, our role is to provide specialized assessments that support safe and well-informed decisions throughout the lifecycle of these assets,” said Marcell Chiarelli , LATAM Executive Commercial Management Director at RINA. articles.title: Woodside to cut more than 500 jobs in $400m savings drive
articles.summary: Australian energy giant Woodside is planning to cut more than 500 jobs worldwide as part of a restructuring programme aimed at delivering $400m in annual cost savings from 2028. The workforce reduction, equivalent to more than 10% of the company’s employees at the end of 2025, forms part of a broader effort to...
articles.body: Offshore Woodside to cut more than 500 jobs in $400m savings drive Bojan Lepic November 5, 2026 1 467 1 minute read Woodside Woodside Australian energy giant Woodside is planning to cut more than 500 jobs worldwide as part of a restructuring programme aimed at delivering $400m in annual cost savings from 2028. The workforce reduction, equivalent to more than 10% of the company’s employees at the end of 2025, forms part of a broader effort to streamline operations, reduce external spending and reshape its oil and gas portfolio. Woodside chief executive Liz Westcott outlined the measures during the company’s Capital Markets Day in Sydney on Thursday. The latest savings target represents a $50m increase from the $350m previously announced and will be measured against the company’s 2025 cost base. Woodside expects the workforce reductions to take place over time but has not disclosed which operations or countries will be affected. According to its latest annual workforce figures, the company employed 4,693 people at the end of 2025, including 3,717 in Australia. Besides reducing employee numbers, Woodside intends to simplify internal processes, improve supply chain management and expand the use of artificial intelligence and digital technologies. The restructuring follows portfolio changes involving its Calypso, Sunrise and Bonaparte carbon capture and storage interests. Westcott said the company was concentrating investment on its most profitable assets while improving operating efficiency and capital discipline. The measures come as Woodside prepares to bring several major developments online. Its Scarborough LNG project offshore Western Australia is 99% complete, with the first LNG cargo expected before the end of 2026. The deepwater Trion oil development offshore Mexico is targeting first production in 2028, followed by the Louisiana LNG project in 2029. Woodside expects these developments to support sales growth of more than 30% to approximately 280m barrels of oil equivalent in 2032. The company has also introduced a new shareholder distribution policy targeting payouts of 20% to 40% of adjusted operating cash flow through dividends and potential share buybacks. articles.body: Europe Offshore Renewables Deutsche Windtechnik lands maintenance deal at Germany’s first offshore wind farm Bojan Lepic November 5, 2026 0 338 1 minute read Alpha Ventus Alpha Ventus German offshore wind services specialist Deutsche Windtechnik has secured a comprehensive maintenance contract from Ocean Breeze Energy covering all 12 turbines at the Alpha Ventus offshore wind farm in the North Sea. The contract will begin in January 2027 and covers turbine servicing, maintenance, troubleshooting and associated technical support. From September 2027, the scope will expand to include remote monitoring, offshore coordination centre services, grid management and around-the-clock alarm handling. The agreement follows Ocean Breeze Energy’s acquisition of Alpha Ventus from EWE, RWE, and Vattenfall in October, with the new owner confirming plans to extend operations at the pioneering German offshore wind development. Commissioned in 2010, Alpha Ventus was Germany’s first offshore wind farm and served as an important testing ground for technologies and maintenance practices subsequently adopted across the country’s offshore wind industry. Located approximately 45 km north of Borkum, the 60 MW development comprises six Senvion 5M turbines and six AREVA Multibrid M5000 units. Deutsche Windtechnik previously provided maintenance services at the project, beginning with the Senvion turbines in 2017 and expanding to the AREVA units in 2020. Both contracts expired at the end of 2024. The new agreement will see the company return to the development under its new ownership structure. Ocean Breeze Energy will retain responsibility for higher-level technical design management. The contract also strengthens Deutsche Windtechnik’s offshore operations around Borkum, where it already provides services at the Riffgat and Trianel Windpark Borkum I projects. articles.body: Asia Europe Middle East Offshore Aker Solutions bags engineering deal for Qatar oilfield redevelopment Bojan Lepic November 5, 2026 0 884 1 minute read Aker Solutions Aker Solutions Norwegian offshore engineering group Aker Solutions has received a letter of award from Vietnam’s PTSC Mechanical & Construction for work on QatarEnergy’s Maydan Mahzam oilfield redevelopment project. The contract covers detailed engineering for three major topsides, four jackets and modifications required to connect new facilities with existing offshore infrastructure. Aker Solutions describes the award as sizeable, valuing it between NOK500m and NOK1.5bn ($54m to $162m). The company will carry out engineering work from its offices in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, and Mumbai, India. The award remains subject to a final contract, with Aker Solutions expecting to register the order in its Renewables and Field Development segment during the fourth quarter of 2026. The Maydan Mahzam field lies around 100 km northeast of Qatar’s coastline, in water depths of approximately 40 metres. Discovered in the 1960s, the field began producing in 1965. QatarEnergy is undertaking a major redevelopment to modernise ageing offshore facilities, improve production efficiency and extend the field’s operating life. PTSC M&C secured the project’s first major offshore construction package in September and signed the main contract with QatarEnergy on October 22. The Vietnamese contractor’s responsibilities include engineering, procurement, fabrication, transportation, installation and commissioning of eight offshore structures weighing more than 100,000 tonnes combined. articles.body: Europe Middle East Offshore Renewables HEA Energy snaps up Subsea7’s six-ship heavy transport business Adis Ajdin November 5, 2026 0 1,386 1 minute read Seaway7 Seaway7 Abu Dhabi-based HEA Energy has struck a deal to acquire Subsea7’s heavy transportation business, adding a six-vessel operation to its growing offshore fleet. The transaction will see Subsea7’s offshore renewables arm Seaway7 divest a business comprising five owned and one chartered open-deck semi-submersible heavy transport vessels. The fleet includes Seaway Eagle, Seaway Falcon, Seaway Hawk, Seaway Osprey, Seaway Albatross and the chartered Seaway Swan . The vessels are used to transport offshore wind foundations, substations, jackup rigs, offshore modules and other oversized cargo, with lifting and transportation capabilities covering loads of up to 55,000 tonnes. Financial terms have not been disclosed, with Subsea7 saying the transaction remains subject to customary closing conditions, including regulatory approvals. Completion is expected in the first half of 2027. The sale forms part of the permitted divestments under Subsea7’s merger agreement with Italian offshore contractor Saipem and will trigger a €105m special dividend to Subsea7 shareholders. For HEA Energy, the acquisition marks another major expansion of its offshore vessel business, which has been growing rapidly across the Middle East and Europe. The company was established in 2022 by Hassan Elali, the founder and former executive chairman of Zakher Marine International (ZMI), which was acquired by ADNOC Logistics & Services. HEA has been building up its offshore support and wind maintenance fleet through newbuildings and acquisitions. By September this year, the company had 19 vessels delivered and another 12 under construction, with deliveries scheduled through 2027. Its expansion has also included offshore wind maintenance work in Europe, where the company has secured contracts involving its jackup vessels, including HEA Hercules , which was mobilised for a North Sea campaign earlier this year. The divestment comes as Subsea7 and Saipem work towards their proposed merger to create Saipem7. Brazil’s competition watchdog gave conditional clearance to the combination on November 4, requiring the separate sale of the Seven Borealis pipelay and heavylift vessel to address competition concerns. The proposed merger, which would create an offshore engineering group with combined revenues of about €21bn ($23.6bn), still faces regulatory scrutiny in Europe and Australia. articles.title: Finland jails captain and crew member over Baltic cable sabotage
articles.summary: A Finnish court has sentenced the captain and a crew member of the general cargo ship Fitburg to prison for deliberately damaging two subsea telecommunications cables in the Gulf of Finland on New Year’s Eve last year. Helsinki District Court handed Russian captain Andrei Maksimenko a three-and-a-half-year prison...
articles.body: Europe Operations Regulatory Finland jails captain and crew member over Baltic cable sabotage Adis Ajdin November 5, 2026 0 20,783 2 minutes read Finnish Border Guard Finnish Border Guard A Finnish court has sentenced the captain and a crew member of the general cargo ship Fitburg to prison for deliberately damaging two subsea telecommunications cables in the Gulf of Finland on New Year’s Eve last year. Helsinki District Court handed Russian captain Andrei Maksimenko a three-and-a-half-year prison sentence, while Azerbaijani bosun Vusal Majidov received two years and 10 months after both were convicted of aggravated criminal damage. The court ordered the two men, who had been subject to travel bans during proceedings, to be taken into custody immediately. They were also ordered to pay compensation for the damage caused to subsea infrastructure. The case centres on the St Vincent and the Grenadines-flagged Fitburg , which was intercepted by Finnish authorities on December 31, 2025, while sailing from St Petersburg to Israel carrying steel products. Investigators established that the vessel had dragged its damaged anchor and chain along the seabed for around 130 km, damaging two telecommunications cables belonging to Elisa and Arelion Finland. The anchor also crossed seven other telecommunications and power cables and a gas pipeline, creating a risk of further damage to critical infrastructure. The court found that the anchor had been lowered after the ship departed St Petersburg but before it left Russian territorial waters. Although prosecutors did not claim that the captain had personally ordered the anchor lowered, the court ruled that both men must have known it was dragging while the vessel continued its voyage. It also found that the bosun had actively contributed to the ship continuing for around two hours after Finnish authorities first contacted the vessel. Both defendants denied wrongdoing and challenged Finland’s jurisdiction, arguing that the damage occurred outside its territorial waters. The court rejected that argument, ruling that Finnish courts could hear the case because the offences were intentional and their consequences were felt in Finland. The decision comes after a separate case involving the Cook Islands-flagged tanker Eagle S , whose crew faced charges over damage to five undersea cables in December 2024. Helsinki District Court initially dismissed that case on jurisdictional grounds in October 2025, but an appeals court overturned the decision in August this year and ordered the case to be reconsidered. The Fitburg defendants were also charged with aggravated interference with telecommunications, but the court dismissed that separate count because it was covered by the aggravated criminal damage conviction. The ruling is not final. The captain’s lawyer has indicated that he intends to appeal, while the bosun is also considering challenging the verdict. articles.body: Asia Greater China Tankers Seacon snaps up fresh tanker in $19.6m deal Adis Ajdin November 5, 2026 0 463 1 minute read Seacon Seacon Hong Kong-listed Seacon Shipping has struck a $19.6m deal for a newly built oil and chemical tanker, adding to its fleet amid reports of a four-vessel MR tanker disposal. The Qingdao-based owner’s Singapore subsidiary has agreed to acquire the 4,981 gt Jia Yue Ming Zhu , which was built in October this year and will be renamed Golden Canna. The vessel is being purchased from Marshall Islands-incorporated Sanhe Jiaye, according to a filing with the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. Seacon will pay a $2.94m deposit upon delivery, with the remaining $16.66m due within 120 days. The acquisition will be funded through internal resources and external financing. The latest purchase follows shipbroking reports linking Seacon to the sale of four MR product tankers in an en bloc deal involving two recently completed vessels and another two still under construction. The company has not publicly confirmed the reported transaction. Seacon has been actively reshaping its tanker portfolio, combining investments in newer chemical and product carriers with vessel sales and refinancing deals. In June, the company agreed to acquire two chemical and oil tankers, Golden Gerbera and Golden Osmanthus , from Oriental Prime Shipping for $39.2m, or $19.6m apiece. The owner also carried out a $103.4m refinancing of four 18,500 dwt chemical tankers in August, replacing earlier sale-and-leaseback arrangements with new 10-year facilities at lower financing margins. Seacon’s push into larger product tankers dates back to 2024, when it contracted four 50,000 dwt MR vessels at Chengxi Shipyard for around $45m each. The group was subsequently linked to another four MR newbuildings through a joint venture with Huanghai Shipbuilding. At the end of June, Seacon controlled 38 vessels and held investments in another 15 through joint ventures, with its diversified portfolio including 18 oil and chemical tankers.
